speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSALS FOR CONSIDERATION BY INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE IN 1946
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to
table copies of proposals for expansion of world trade and employment which were communicated by' the United States government, together with the text of a financial agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States, as signed at Washington on December 6, 1945, and related documents. These are in printed forms.
In connection with the tabling of these documents there is a brief statement I should like to make.
Trade and Employment

These proposals have been prepared for consideration by an international conference on trade and employment, which the United States government suggests should be convened by the united nations organization for the summer of 1946.
The government of the United States has proposed that all countries should concert their efforts in the sphere of their international economic relations, with a view to expanding the volume of world trade and maintaining high and stable levels of national employment. The specific suggestions for achieving these ends, set forth in the document which is now being tabled for the consideration of members of parliament, deserve our most careful study, for no country has a greater interest than Canada in the realization of these objectives.
Members of the house will recall that in withdrawing, on November 12 last, such tariff changes as had been incorporated in the budget resolutions the Minister of Finance stated that "within the last few days we have been given substantial ground for believing that the prospects of early international action for the reduction of tariffs and other barriers to world trade are considerably improved." The documents I am tabling to-day indicate that in the four weeks that have intervened, material progress has been made and that what was then a mere hope or expectation has become, to quote from the joint statement by President Truman and Prime Minister Attlee, "agreement on the broad principles of commercial policy for which the two governments will seek international support."

employees back to work we urge that the proposal made by the Honourable Mr. Daley and myself in our letter of November 27 be again put before your membership by referendum vote.
Both sides have now agreed that in calling men back to work seniority rules shall prevail as far as this is possible under the circumstances. If the Departments of Labour of the dominion and Ontario governments can be of assistance in the supervision of such vote we shall be very willing to arrange such assistance.

I wish to call to the attention of the minister a situation which exists, I think, peculiarly in

Alberta and which I think should be remedied, certainly not later than the next session. Out there, still being under the Northwest Territories Act, on a charge of murder the defence is allowed but six challenges. The crown on the other hand have six challenges and-I forget the number-it is thirty or forty "stand asides", at least that is the expression which has come to be used. The net position is just this, that if a man is charged with murder and a jury is being selected he can object to only six people, while the crown on the other hand is able to eliminate about fifty. Now it may be said that both have an equal number of challenges, but as the minister well knows, a "stand aside" is equivalent to a challenge so far as the person on the panel acting on that jury is concerned. I have had personal experience of this within the last six weeks or twelve months. In the case of a man charged with murder I used my six challenges, and then the crown simply went ahead and selected those jurors that they sought. I am not suggesting that there was anything wrong in what crown counsel did; he is an able man and a close personal friend; but I do say that that is a situation which in my judgment is simply crying for a remedy. I do not think that any member of the committee, knowing the seriousness of the crime with which such a man is charged, would wish to put him at any disadvantage whatever. The whole scheme of our administration of justice is that every consideration should be given to an accused person.
It may be that this is something in respect of which the provincial government should be consulted, although I do not think so. It is something over which they have no jurisdiction. I know they would expect to be consulted with respect to numbers of jurors and things of that kind, but I can think of no reason why they should expect to be consulted with respect to the number of challenges. In short, I am asking that we be put in just the same position as the other provinces and come under the criminal code with respect to challenges and selection of jurors in general.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I can assure the hon. member of my full sympathy with the object he has in view in the remarks he has made this morning. I give him the further assurance that his suggestion will be carefully .considered, and if it is found that it is something we can do at once it will be attended to. If it should be felt that the attorney general of his province should be consulted, we will do that.

Some short time ago the
Minister of Justice made a statement regarding penitentiaries, to the effect that when a riot or disturbance took place in a penitentiary the request had been made to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation not to broadcast the information throughout the country. Anyone who has had to do with penitentiaries or has made visits to them realizes that in the various penitentiaries there are radios; these men are listening to what is going on, and the report of a disturbance or riot in one penitentiary does affect or might affect others. But it was reported in the press the other day that, the new appointee to the head of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had said: Despite what the Minister of Justice or the department has requested, we will broadcast any riot that takes place throughout the country. I know there is a tendency to set up bureaucratic bodies and say to parliament: Hands off; no political interference. That is [DOT]all right, but to my w'ay of thinking there is a new danger arising in this country, of setting up dictators in charge of boards and bureaux who are defying the very will of the people. Here is the first that has arisen, and I am asking the Minister of Justice to take note of the statement of the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, who says in effect that whether it is in the public interest or not, he as chairman will broadcast these things, and the Minister of Justice can go to the dickens. It is time this parliament, which is the voice of the people, resolved that this new dictatorship should not be allowed to go much farther than it has gone.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	I think the hon.
member is under a misapprehension as to this new dictatorship." Mr. Dunton was appointed chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and he communicated with me the other day to inform me that at a meeting of the governors a resolution had been passed to the effect that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation could not refrain from broadcasting all news which was available to the newspapers and to the other broadcasting corporations. The resolution of the governors has been received, and there has been no opportunity as yet to give it consideration. But I should not like the impression to go out that this is a one-man decision of the new chairman of the board; and I can assure the hon. member that the resolution of the board of governors will be given careful consideration.

With reference to the
reclamation of prisoners sent to penitentiaries in Canada, a year ago I had an experience with a young man who had been committed to one of these institutions. I will not say which one, because that is neither here nor there; they are all in the same boat as far as that is concerned. Before being sent to prison he had worked in a butcher shop, and his mother was anxious that he should learn something more about butchering while in the penitentiary. I wrote to the warden conveying that request to him. Later I read an article in one of the publications put out in Toronto -I believe it was Hush. At any rate, it was one of those publications that do some good. I do not know how Hush got hold of the information, but there was an article about this young man not having been given an opportunity to learn the butchering trade in the penitentiary. That was the first I had heard about his having been turned down.
I remember well some years ago the minister's predecessor, the Hon. Ernest Lapointe, brought in a bill, and he said that without penitentiary reform he could not remain minister of justice. He said the situation was intolerable. Following that speech I myself went over to England to study prison reform, particularly with reference to the Borstal system. I studied the system as it existed in the prison near Leeds. I believe it was at Leeds that the Borstal system was organized. I learned that the system had done fine work. I should like to find out what programme we have for prison reform or for the reclaiming of prisoners in our penitentiaries. I am not one of those who believe that prisoners should be released indiscriminately. Possibly there are some who cannot be reclaimed, but I believe that there are many who can. What is the department doing along the Borstal line or in any other direction looking to the reclaiming of prisoners?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Apparently, in spite of the fact that the hon. member is a constant attendant at debates in the house, he must have nodded when the amendment to the Penitentiaries Act was being debated and when it was passed in this house a couple of weeks ago. On that occasion the matter was gone into fully-

I remember that.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: -and an amendment to the Penitentiaries Act was put through to enable the government to appoint at once one commissioner to do the preparatory work of implementing as far as possible the Archam-bault. report under the jurisdiction of the
Supply-Justice

federal parliament. I said then that it was hoped there might be an opportunity during the dominion-provincial conference to discuss carrying it even farther than could be done under the jurisdiction the dominion now has over penitentiaries.
With respect to the case the hon. member mentions, I am sorry I am not a reader of Hush, and I do not know anything about it. But even under the present set-up it is the aim of wardens to see that training as effective and appropriate as possible is provided for those who are interned under their charge. I should be glad if the hon. member would give me the particulars in the case he mentions, because it would appear from what he says that something has gone wrong. I should like to have the case investigated and brought to the attention not only of the warden of the penitentiary in question but of the wardens of all penitentiaries in order to make them more careful in applying the policy, namely, of doing the best we can in the way of training and rehabilitation for convicted persons.
I hope that ere long there will have been selected a competent person to take on the job of going as far as possible with the implementing of the recommendations of the Archambault commission. It was not possible to do that during the war because of the shortage both of material and of man-power, but we have now reached the point where I hope both competent man-power and building material required for the purpose of carrying out these very commendable recommendations will be available.

Do these recommendations envisage some such programme as the Borstal system?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The Borstal system could not properly be installed by the federal government, with the limited jurisdiction it has over penitentiaries. One of the purposes in trying to get a proper person as chairman of the commission is to have someone who will visit the attorneys general and discuss the situation in each of the provinces with a view to having all the governments do, in that direction, that which will be of benefit to the Canadian public by more effective rehabilitation programmes in dealing with persons who happen to fall by the wayside.

The matter I wish to
refer to arises out of the observations of the hon. member for New Westminster. There is another side to the question he has raised. He complains of some display of dictatorship on the part of the general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with

regard to the broadcasting of information relating to riots and other troubles in the penitentiaries. The other aspect of the matter is this. Although this sort of news has been appearing in the press regularly, and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, through its facilities, arranges with the Canadian Press to carry that kind of news along with other news, apparently some directive was issued by the Department of Justice to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation instructing them to discontinue broadcasts of the kind1. I would respectfully invite the Minister of Justice to state what form of directive or instruction was issued by his department to the broadcasting corporation in connection with the discontinuance of broadcasts of news of that sort. I should like later to make a comment on it, but that information is due the house and the Canadian people because there has been some misunderstanding and a good many questions are being asked by the public as to the circumstances under which such directive or instruction was issued by the Department of Justice, to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No directive or instruction was issued by the department to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It so happened that when the matter arose I took it up with the manager of the corporation. For the reasons that I put before him I obtained his compliance with a request that he ask the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to refrain from broadcasting that kind of news at the hours when the news broadcasts are allowed to be received in the penitentiaries. There was no directive; there were no instructions; there is no ground for alarm. It was a request that was made, and at the time they considered that the reasons for it were sufficient to justify the granting of the request. The board of governors have come to a different conclusion and the matter has not been further discussed.
When the request was made the staffs of the penitentiaries were as much restricted as it had been possible to make them because we had given leave of absence to large numbers of guards and others who wished to enlist in the armed forces. At that time I felt that it was a reasonable request to make, and the then manager of the broadcasting corporation felt that it was a reasonable request to accede to. The matter was mentioned here the other day when we were discussing the penitentiaries bill. It immediately raised a hue and cry and a storm of protest about the censorship that was to be exercised over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The governors in

Supply-Justice
solemn session passed a resolution that they would not submit to that. That resolution has been received and has not yet been considered. That is the whole story so far.

Would the minister
indicate what the policy of the department is likely to be now in view of the stand taken by the board of governors of the broadcasting corporation? I am not pressing this in any carping way, but since the matter has implications that may be more far-reaching than one is inclined to realize the committee might properly ask the minister for some indication of policy in the matter. It is indicated that the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have asserted their right to continue these broadcasts notwithstanding the request from the minister. What policy does the minister propose to follow with reference to this matter and similar broadcasts of information?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The minister and the department propose to do their best to maintain order in the penitentiaries. The minister and the department know from experience that when news of trouble in one penitentiary penetrates into another it is disturbing. Now, as to what measures we shall have to adopt to prevent that cause of disturbance, no decision has yet been reached. It may be that we shall have to have some kind of filtering or monitoring system to prevent news that would be the cause of disturbances in the penitentiaries from getting in there. The simplest way seemed to be to prevent it from going on the air, but apparently there is strong objection to that method being adopted. Wre are certainly going to try to find some method of preventing that cause of disturbance in the penitentiaries.

I do not want to pursue the matter further, but I hope that some method can be worked out by the Department of Justice for doing what is necessary to preserve proper discipline within the penitentiaries without its becoming necesary to ask the broadcasting corporation to refrain from putting over the air waves information that is circulating freely in the press. I do not agree with the view expressed by the hon. member for New Westminster that it is evidence of dictatorship on the part of the C.B.C. when they assert the right to put over the air waves information that is published freely in the press. I rather think that in a situation of this kind the board of governors are to be commended for their determination to see that the same freedom exists on the air waves as exists in the press in the matter of the
distribution of news. It is not evidence of dictatorship on the part of the C.B.C.; it is evidence that the C.B.C. appreciates its full responsibility to the public, regardless of whatever request may be received from the government. I think it is evidence of independent judgment in these matters on the part of the C.B.C. andi an unwillingness to yield meekly to a request from a minister of the crown. It is highly important that in the broadcasting of news that the freedom of the C.B.C. be preserved, just as we want the freedom of the press to be preserved in regard to the printing of news.

In answer to the hon. member (Mr. Fleming) may I say my chief reason for bringing the matter before the committee at this time was not to show that the C.B.C. or the manager was not attending to any directive or not paying attention to any directive, because I know that that body has been set up as a body independent of parliament. What I was objecting to was the request itself and what lay behind it. If the governors of the C.B.C. would investigate and speak to the wardens of the penitentiaries they would find out the truth. The warden in New Westminster told me that every time the news of a disturbance in a penitentiary comes over the air he has to put on extra guards. He can sense the feeling of the convicts and has to take extra precautions against trouble that may arise because that news has come over the radio. If the C.B.C. had looked into that matter and made an inquiry they might have taken this stand. While the minister has no right to give any direction to us and no right to expect that we will take it, the matter is worthy of attention.
When I mentioned the word "dictatorship," what I had in mind, and what I was objecting to, was this. I do not know whether the hon. member is aware of what we have been up against. We have many boards to-day, and when we think we have a real injustice and go to them they say: "We do not care about that; parliament has set us up as an independent bod}'." When we go to the minister and mention these things he says: "Do not speak to me; I have nothing at all to do with that; parliament has set up that particular body"; and so we are drifting and losing our democracy and freedom. There are hundreds of other instances of the kind. I shall have something to say about the C.B.C. and what they are doing when we come to the appropriate item.
I just want to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in this country we are drifting away from democracy and

losing our freedom. The members who represent the people are being ruthlessly shoved to one side by members of these boards.

There were two or three questions I wanted to ask the minister, but with regard to the last matter just mentioned I think the minister acted somewhat indiscreetly in communicating with the general manager. I was glad to hear the hon. member for New Westminster speaking as he did. What I rose to speak about was something that the minister mentioned the other day. I realize the difficulties. In Canada to-day we have a definite crime wave, as they have in the United States.
And in Great Britain, too.

In Great Britain, too, as my hon. friend says. It is becoming very serious. The multiplication of robberies with violence by men who commit murder warrants serious consideration. When men carry revolvers, pistols and the like they go out prepared to commit murder. I was surprised when I read the other day the extent to which revolvers and pistols are legally held by Canadians. The extent of what I call an evil-excepting where the carrying of guns is absolutely necessary-is appalling. According to the last registration there are over 222,000 revolvers legally owned in this dominion. This means there is a great bank available for thugs and desperadoes to be able to put themselves, by means of theft, in possession of the instruments of their profession. While I am far from advocating the use of unfair or strong-arm methods, I for one cannot see the need for that number of revolvers in this dominion, available, as I said a moment ago, as a bank to potential wrongdoers.
What consideration, I ask the minister, has been given to ostracizing the revolver and pistol in this country, removing them from the hands of all except those who require them and will properly guard their possession?

The prospect facing us is fearful, when week by week, in spite of heavier sentences, robbery with violence is so much on the increase. These men cannot operate without revolvers and pistols. Shotguns are of no use to them at all because they are too easily seen. The onl}' order in council I know anything about in this connection, and I obtained this information from the Department of Justice, is the one that was passed on July 23 last having to do with the regulation of weapons being brought back to Canada as war weapons, mementoes and war trophies. Has the minister given consideration to stringent legislation, or, if we have not time to pass such, legislation at this session, an order in council, to banish the revolver as an instrument in the hands of people in this country, other than those who require it?
The situation in the old country, as the Minister of Labour stated, is most serious. 'The same can be said of the United States where, though their position is different from ours because of state rights, they are contemplating measures to take away from potential murderers their instruments and the insignia of their profession, as it were. I Should like very much to hear the minister speak on this. I realize that he has given a great deal of thought to it, and anything he might propose I am sure would receive support right across this country. We do not want to see anything approaching regimentation; we are all in agreement on that, but this is not a case of regimentation. It is a case of the safety of the state in time of peace.

Mr. Chairman, I have several observations to make on our penal system, and I think this is as good a time as any to make them. I notice there is another items on branch administration, but I had proposed to give this talk some time ago, and I feel that what I shall put before the committee is worthy of some consideration at this time. I have no apologies to make for taking up the time of the committee, because penal reform is a matter of major importance.
There is no doubt that the most effective method of dealing with young offenders, and we have plenty of them, is the application of the Borstal system which is used in the United Kingdom. The Archambault. royal commission report advocated the adoption in Canada of the principles of this system. During the war years no attempt was made to implement many of these recommendations, especially the one with regard to Borstal institutions. The war was generally accepted as an adequate reason for inaction on the part of the government. However, now that the war is over I submit that there is no further reason for delay. A careful examination of the 19-15-46 estimates under the services enumerated for the penitentiaries branch does not disclose any item that indicates any real attempt to implement the important recommendations made in the report of the royal commission, especially those with regard to Borstal schools. It has been suggested, and rightly so, that this federal capital has a high rating as a last resting place of royal commission reports.
The royal commission to investigate penal reform in Canada cost this country $108,719. It is the opinion of sincere students of penology, men who are not cranks but scientists and practical sociologists, that that report is one of the most noteworthy pronouncements on penal matters ever made by a responsible body in this country. The work was thorough, the calibre of the men on the commission was of the highest order, and the cost was not excessive provided that something is done about reforming our prison inmates. Otherwise the public may rightly assume that this expenditure was a waste of public money.
I submit that for every day that this nation delays in making the necessary reforms for

the proper rehabilitation of the convicts in our prisons, it is paying dearly in wasted dollars, repeated crimes and unredeemed human life. The failure to modernize and to humanize our penal institutions is poor business. This country spends millions to perpetuate a system of crime schools. Because of their very nature our prisons fail to rehabilitate and reform the young offender. We are creating a criminal class by schooling them in the practice and technique of crime. Institutions such as we have fail to correct or cure; they are an expensive liability. According to United Kingdom and Canada year books, the rate of crime in this country as compared with England and Wales is four to one. Our crime convictions increased three hundred per cent between 1901 and 1935, and they are still increasing. Adult convictions per hundred thousand in Canada in 1900 were 109, but by 1940 they had increased to 452 per hundred thousand.
Are those convictions for crime, or do they cover convictions for violations of traffic laws and so on?

Those are penitentiary
offences.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Does the hon. member assert that those are convictions to penitentiary terms?
They are major convictions. If the sentence exceeds two years the man goes to the penitentiary, but these are still major crimes. Most of these are recidivists.
Is the hon. member sure he is correct?

Absolutely correct.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Is the hon. member
saying that the statistics he is giving are of persons convicted to serve terms in the penitentiary?

This information is taken from "Penal Institutions", by Topping. That is the statement made by Mr. Topping, who is a much greater expert in this field than L am. Most convicts are repeaters or, as they are called, recidivists. Three out of four males admitted to our penal institutions in 1943 and 1944, according to this same authority, had been previously convicted1 of crime. That is roughly seventy-five per cent.

Has the hon. member figures pertaining to the results of the inquiry into the Borstal system of preventing repeaters?

Supply-Justice

Yes, and I will give that information as I go along. Obviously, if these figures are accurate, and there is no reason to believe they are not, we are failing to reform our criminals. In 1925, 1,702 of the inmates in our penal institutions had been convicted three or more times, but by 1936 this figure had risen to 8,060, an alarming increase of almost 500 per cent. This should be a matter of serious concern. It does not matter whether they went to gaol or to a major penal institution under federal jurisdiction; the fact remains that the increase has been 500 per cent.
Penologists are alarmed, too, at the increase in the number of youths who are committed for breaches of the law. In 1931 there were 1,324' offenders between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one convicted for indictable offences, just five times the number in the United Kingdom, with four times our population. In 1943 according to the Canada Year Book, 53-3 per cent of our prison inmates were under thirty years of age.
Our penal institutions are costing this country millions of dollars. Apprehending the criminal and the maintenance of police and law courts cost many millions more. Tables have been compiled to show the cost to the country of 188 repeaters, selected from a group of 8,000 of these unfortunates. The number of convictions against these 188 was 3,434, or an average of 19 per person; 2,636 were major convictions, which cost an estimated $18,005 per prisoner. There were 798 minor convictions registered, which cost an average of $948 per person. The average cost of keeping each prisoner was $1,463 for gaol and reformatories, and $5,984 for penitentiaries. Without reckoning the loss to citizens occasioned by the crimes committed or the funds devoted to the relief of dependents or the economic loss to the nation because of the incarceration of these individuals, these 188 repeaters cost the country in gaol and reformatory costs, $264,876; penitentiary maintenance, $1,083,254; and cost of convictions, $3,258,960, or a total of $4,607,090, which amounts to an average cost of $25,453 per repeater, and at the same time prevention and welfare agencies spent $10 per head to aid or redeem these unfortunates. Surely we are penny wise and pound foolish.
Furthermore, costs are increasing; for according to the 1942 report of the superintendent of penitentiaries it cost $1.98 per day in 1941 for the maintenance of each prison inmate, and in the next year, 1942, the cost had risen to $2.18 per day. Last year the estimates of this government show that in 47696-211i	,
the province of Ontario alone, for the maintenance of judges and law courts, which are a part of the machinery of justice for the handling of criminal cases we spent $5J million.
Why do wc have repeaters? One of the main reasons is that inmates are still permitted to mingle with one another-the youthful offender with the seasoned criminal. Furthermore the opportunity of educating and training these inmates is denied because they are unable to take that training under the conditions prevailing in our institutions at the present time. And the result is that when these young people come out of our penitentiaries they are not equipped to maintain themselves. Much of the training that is required is denied because of the inadequacy of accommodation in our prison institutions. I suggest further that it may be because of the lack of trained personnel to train and advise these young people.
In reply to a question which I put on the order paper the Minister of Justice replied on October 31 to the effect that 137 changes as recommended by the royal commission had been implemented. But these changes were mostly of a minor nature and to ease the hardships of some prisoners does not change the punitive and repressive nature of our prison regime. One major recommendation, the installation of the Borstal system, has not. been acted upon.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: And cannot be acted upon until there is some change in our constitution.
Mr. McKAY; The failure to act promptly on this particular recommendation means that young people are still leaving our prisons worse members of society than when they entered. This is a severe indictment of our system but wholly justified by the results.
They were not very good members of society when they went into those institutions.

No, they were not. To permit the young offender to associate with the hardened criminal has brought disastrous consequences. This is well illustrated in an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on July 23, 1944. I shall not take time to read it, but the editorial refers to a young girl who was convicted of a minor offence, driving a motor car at an excessive rate of speed. When she got out of prison she made the charge that the gaol was a school of crime, and she claimed that from the knowledge she acquired while there she is now

Yes, and the police are investigating.

I believe it was. It takes a lot of time to answer questions, Mr. Chairman, and I do njot wish to take up too much of the time of the committee.

I preface the few remarks I wish to make with regard to the occupation of judges by asking the minister if he is in a position to say how many judges appointed by federal authority are at present engaged in work on commissions or in any other work outside the pursuit of their ordinary judicial duties, and if he can also give the same information for the past five years.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have not that information. I know there are some judges who have been appointed to commissions. Some of them have completed the work they were asked to do and some have not. I presume I could get the information, but I am sorry to say I have not got it here.

I would like to suggest to the committee that the practice of appointing judges to commissions where the questions at issue are not judicial-they are sometimes social and frequently tinged1 with politics- has been indulged in not only by the present administration or by the one which preceded it. Both major parties have resorted to this practice, and it is because I believe that the practice is an improper one that I wish to draw it in a particular way to the attention of the minister.
This morning we heard the Minister of Labour refer to the possibility of appointing a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada to compose a conflict between capital and labour which for several months has baffled all agencies which have attempted to compose it. It is true that the Canadian people have great confidence in their judiciary, and it is well that it should be thus. But I submit that the continuation of this practice will undermine, and I am sorry to say that in my opinion it is already undermining, the respect that our people have for our judiciary. I shall refrain from mentioning particular instances, but there is no man who is familiar with the administration of justice in Canada who cannot, within his own personal experience of the last few years, pick out instances in which the judiciary has been drawn into controversies which were far from being judicial, controversies which in the result have tagged this judge as one favourable to capital, this judge as one favourable to labour, this judge as favourable to one political party and this judge to another, this judge as favourable to one fiscal or financial theory and this other judge as favourable to an opposite theory. This I think is highly reprehensible and regrettable. We have a number of institutions in the country of which we are very proud, and of none are the Canadian people more proud and more justly proud than of its judiciary. The practice of taking men away from their judicial functions to hold a semipolitical problem in abeyance, pending the formation of a policy which may prove a solvent for it, is highly unfortunate. It not only results in the deterioration of the respect that Canadians have for their judges: it delays the administration of justice. Judges

taken away from their duties are not replaced and the administration of justice frequently suffers.
I am confident that the minister is aware of many such instances, and it is quite probable they have been drawn to his attention. Judges are frequently not unwilling to accept these additional tasks because it sometimes affords them an opportunity for increasing a remuneration which in my opinion is entirely inadequate. If our judges received a compensation which enabled them to live on a plane commensurate with the importance of duties they perform, it is quite possible that the temptation to take on this additional extra judicial work would not be as great, and it might enable the members of the judiciaiy to resist the temptation to augment in this way their totally insufficient salaries.
I therefore ask the minister if it is not possible to put an end to this practice, which has, as a direct result, the slowing down of the administration of justice in all jurisdictions and the exposure of the judiciary to a loss of reputation for impartiality which is so essential to the maintenance of the administration of justice on the high plane on which it has always been in Canada.

In a moment I am going to disagree with many of the things that the hon. member for Stanstead has said. You see, there is some independence in this group over here. First I want to make a suggestion to the minister in connection with this revolver and pistol business. It may be foolish, but it may have some merit. Can we not help the situation by having complete restrictions, or at least tightly drawn restrictions, on the sale of ammunition? We have all these guns in the country, and it seems reasonable to suppose that in a comparatively short length of time the ammunition that a man brought back in his pocket will be exhausted through target practice, shooting sparrows, or something of the kind. Unfortunately some of it may be used on ourselves. But in any event within a limited time surely it will be exhausted. My information is that revolver ammunition is of a specialized kind. I take it the idea is that a man who has some crows on his farm may have a shot gun or a rifle, but he does not need something that he can pack in his pocket and probably use on his neighbour. I think that is at the bottom of the whole business. A revolver is not much good if you have nothing to shoot from it.
May I now come to the views expressed by the hon. member for Stanstead. He seems to take issue with something I said in this

Supply-Justice
house some time ago, when, we were dealing with labour. I want to make it plain that my views in that connection are based on this broad principle, namely, the rule of law. Everything that we have in the way of protection of the individual has been obtained by enforcing honesty in business transactions. After all, laws are nothing more than the codification of good sense and good morals. That is all they are at any time, and all that this country has accomplished, at least socially. What does it rest on?	It rests
broad-based on the rule of law. That is the main reason why in labour matters I did suggest an appeal by either party from a board of conciliation to a judge of the supreme court. I go further. Do not worry; I give my hon. frietnd credit for the finest intentions in the world. He is a man of great capacities and long experience. I know quite a number of judges, and I say that in my view they do not accept these assignments with any idea of an increase in income, because all they get is a living allowance. Let me put it in this way: in the province from which I come that is the situation. Why do they do these things?
I do not think they like these assignments, but they do accept them as a matter of public duty. Say the hon. member for Stanstead and I have a lawsuit, and I go before the hon. member for Lake Centre who some day will be the chief justice of an important part of this country. Suppose I lose my lawsuit to my friend over here; my first reaction will be to damn gently the hon. member for Lake Centre. That is just human nature. We think he is no good. But we get over that after the first blush on losing, because no one likes to lose; after that passes the thing goes on.
What is the great value of a court of law in civil business? It is this. We hope that the judgments are right, but we know that, the judgment having been given, the business of the country can proceed. It seems to me that that is a consideration which is not given sufficient attention.
On the political side I want to say this. We will assume that in another election, were I to run, which I am not going to do, I was beaten and dissatisfied, and I had the opportunity of picking my judge. I would accept the judge who before he was appointed to the bench was of a political persuasion other than my own. Why? For this very good reason, that I know of nothing to which judges are so sensitive as the suggestion that they may have political bias. My experience, and it is somewhat broad, is that rather than have anybody think anything of the kind, and in order to be perfectly straight, they will lean
backwards in the other direction. May I go with the hon. member, though, and go with him a long way in this? We do not pay our judges nearly enough. What is the result? We will say that there are a number of people who would accept an appointment to the bench, but many of them simply cannot do it. Why not? They have a scale of living to which they have become accustomed, a family to clothe, educate and so on, and they simply cannot do it

they cannot make a quick reduction in income; let me put it in that way.
I refer to that scale of living as something which grew normally from the money they earned, and they cannot just drop down in that scale and carry on their ordinary duties to their family and friends.
I am happy to say that I had the opportunity of a chat with the Minister of Justice on this question the other day. I know he is in entire agreement with the views I have expressed. He had expressed them before in this house on two occasions.

I intended to say a few words on the matter that was spoken to by the hon. member for Lake Centre, namely, the crime wave and how to control it. I am not going to deal with the control of firearms. I realize that it is a difficult problem, because the firearms which are generally used in crimes are, I suppose, those which are not registered. The department knows where the registered firearms are and can confiscate them, but it does not know where the firearms are that are not registered.
The crime wave which has struck this country in the last year or two is not peculiar to Canada. I notice from the press that it is world-wide. In the press yesterday I saw that Scotland Yard had made an appeal to the people of Britain to assist. A few day9 ago I read that Moscow was in pretty much the same position, and the same is true of the United States. We must conclude therefore that this crime wave has developed out of the way of life of so 'many people during the past five or six years. This being so I do not think we can remedy the situation by statutes or laws or regulations. It can be overcame ultimately only by leading our people into more constructive ways of life, giving them obligations and opportunities to carry out those obligations, and in this way building up their responsibilities. In my opinion we can never eliminate crimes of violence or any other sort of crimes against society by laws and penitentiaries and prisons and police and all that sort of thing. We can do it only by building up in our people a sense of obligation to the community. In the past I think we have placed too much em-
Supply-Justice

phasis on our rights without at the same time emphasizing our obligations. But it follows that if we are to put people in a position to lead constructive and useful lives, they must feel that others consider them to be useful and decent members of society. I know of nothing that will help a person have greater regard for his honour and integrity than to feel that other people believe in him. That is all I want to say on this point.
In regard to the controversy between the hon. member for Calgary West and the hon. member for Stanstead in the matter of judges acting in labour disputes-
Not only labour disputes; all extra-judicial work.

I will deal with the labour dispute point, because it is the one with which I am most familiar. I think that generally speaking, organized labour has more confidence in a court or board presided over by an eminent judge than in a board presided over by anyone else, and we should have such courts and boards where the judges are chosen with great care. But I do not believe it would be a good policy to allow appeals from boards of that kind to any judge or court. These cases should be confined to labour courts only, and these decisions should not be referred to any judge outside that court.

I can readily understand the desire of a man to retain as a souvenir a weapon he had used or had captured on the battlefield, but seldom would he wish to use that weapon after obtaining it. I suggest that such weapons could be made ineffective by any armourer or gunsmith at the time of registration, which might possibly prevent them from falling into the hands of criminals.

There was one matter I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister in connection with the administration of justice in Saskatchewan. A six man jury system was brought into effect in that province about 1932 as a result of a request by the then Saskatchewan government. This change was made with a view to saving money through a reduction in jury fees. The same system was adopted in one or more other provinces in the middle west. I think it is generally agreed that the six men jury system has not worked out as satisfactorily as the traditional twelve men jury. There is something about the twelve men jury that is lacking in a jury with lesser numbers. The exercise of control by a judge is more definite in the case of the smaller jury. Tradition and experience have shown that a jury of twelve men is the ideal number. Has the minister had under consideration the amendment of the criminal code to enable Saskatchewan to return to the old system of twelve men juries? Representations were made at the last two meetings of the Saskatchewan Bar Association, but I am not certain whether those have been transmitted to the minister with a view to an amendment of the criminal code.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Dealing only with the last question of the hon. member for Lake Centre, may I say that I have no knowledge of any representations having been received from the government or the attorney general of Saskatchewan. I should not like to initiate any change that was not suggested by the attorney general, who is of course primarily responsible for the administration of justice in his province. If I may be permitted, I would suggest that the resolutions of the 47696-212
Saskatchewan Bar Association be brought to the attention of the attorney general of the province. I can assure my hon. friend that if the attorney general will in turn bring them to our attention and suggest that he would like to have them dealt with, careful consideration will be given to them.
If it is not the wish of the committee that this item should carry now, I shall have to ask that it be allowed to stand, because there is a matter of great urgency that requires my presence elsewhere. I shall endeavour to be back in the committee as quickly as possible, when I shall deal with the questions which were raised this morning and with such others as may require attention.

Lands, parks and forests branch-
1ST. Branch administration, $20,000.

Before the war provision was made for national parks in practically every province but New Brunswick. I understand that at that time there was some difficulty with the provincial government over the selection of a site. Has there been any consultation with the provincial government regarding a site, and are steps being taken to establish a national park in New Brunswick?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: The matter is under consideration. The provincial government have two or three sites in view but they have not decided which one they will offer to the dominion government.

That has been the situation for the last six or seven years. Before the war there were two or three sites under consideration, but nothing has been done as yet. Are they still considering two or three different sites, or has the matter been allowed to stand all this time without anything being done?
At the present time the provincial government is considering two or three sites. As soon as they have settled the matter we will then consider the formation of a national park.
Can the minister give the location of the different sites in New Brunswick which are under consideration at the present time?
I have not that information at the moment, but I can get it and give it to the hon. member.

Under what item would aids to road construction be taken up?

Supply-Mines and Resources

That would come under the surveys and engineering branch, item 150.
Mr, ZAPLITNY: Are permits being issued to settlers near Riding Mountain national park to cut timber for lumber purposes, and if so, what price is being charged them per thousand?
The timber in Riding Mountain national park is budgeted each year. Certain areas are set aside and for these permits are granted.
What price is charged to the settlers per thousand?
I have not that figure here, but I can supply it later.

Is there a uniform price charged to all who cut timber in Riding Mountain national park, or is there one price for large contractors who take a timber berth and a different price for the ordinary settler who wishes to get a permit to cut timber in the park?
As the hon. member knows, there have been two timber limits in that park area for many years. But the price to the settlers is uniform.

This is important, Mr. Chairman, because it involves a matter of policy. According to a return that I received from the minister's department on September 11, 1945, there were in the park two timber berths, Nos. 571 and 551D, which have been contracted for by the Northern Trust company. They have taken out since 1940, according to the figures I have here, a total of over 7,000,000 board feet of lumber at a price slightly over $7,000, which works out at one dollar per thousand. At the same time the settlers and people living around the park w'ho wish to take out lumber in smaller lots pay considerably more than that. Why is there this tremendous difference? In the first place I do not think that one dollar per thousand for lumber is very good business on the part of the government. The lumber is worth considerably more than that. I should like to know why there should be any difference in the price charged to the settler who cuts lumber for himself and the price charged to the Northern Trust company.

There are two limits there that were granted long before the park came into being, and the contractors are taking off that timber. As soon as it is cleared', those areas will be taken over by the park. That is the reason for the discrimination. We cannot interfere with what is already a contract with those who purchased these limits prior to the establishment of the park. fMr. Bracken.]
Do I understand the minister to say that the department has no power to alter a contract that was entered into before the area became a park? If that is so, it is strange, to say the least.
That is so; we cannot alter the contract.

Is there any movement to take some provincial parks and bring them under federal jurisdiction? I have in mind Kenosee park. There has been some talk of its being made a national park. Have recommendations to that effect been made to the department?
No recommendations have been made as such. A national park can be established only on land given by the province to the dominion for the purpose.

How far does Wood Buffalo park extend into the Northwest Territories? You start passing the park on the Slave river south of Fort Fitzgerald, which is in northern Alberta. Does the park extend into the Northwest Territories?
There are nearly 14,000 square miles of it in the province of Alberta, 3,625 square miles in the Northwest Territories.
That park in Alberta comes under this department?
Yes.
Has any discussion taken place with British Columbia with regard to taking over Forbidden Plateau as a national park?
Some proposals have been made, but no conclusion has been arrived at. The provincial government is considering the matter and will submit a proposal.

I presume this is the expedition which leaves Nova Scotia every year to take supplies to the northern country?
It leaves from Montreal.

The details show $200 for supplies and materials, and $65,000 for freight, express, telegrams, postage, and so forth. Do other departments supply the materials and goods sent to the northern country, or does it all come under this department?
