Supply-Mines and Resources

Can the minister tell us what plans the government have in mind for checking up and developing the resources in the Northwest Territories? There was a small vote under the war appropriation bill, "Report on resources, etc., of Canada's northwest region, $5,000," which will be found at page 554 of Hansard. One of the most important jobs which the Canadian government has, I think, is to assist in opening up the Northwest Territories. I would ask the minister to let us know what is being done in that connection.

While the vote for general administration shows a decrease of $75,000, the actual expenditures for the year 1944-45 were $372,689. It should be pointed out that there will be included in the supplementary estimates for the current year an item of $553,800 for the Northwest Territories, which will bring the appropriations to $933,485. I mention this for the purpose of informing the members that the government is making provision for increased facilities of many kinds in the territories. The moneys in the supplementary vote are being used for the following purposes:
Yellowknife Airport	 $245,000
Administration and staff buildings	140,000
Additional forest protection ....	140,000
Other improvements and facilities	28,800
Are these in the Yellowknife area?

Yes, chiefly. In addition to these expenditures, considerable moneys from other votes of the department are being expended in developing the resources of the territories. An extensive geological field survey programme has been carried out in the Northwest Territories during the last three years, and this was enlarged during the past season. In addition several topographical parties were in the field, and every effort is being made to have the most important areas properly mapped. As well, the hydrographic service did considerable charting work on the Mackenzie river route to improve water transportation, and also completed the charting of the Yellowknife bay area in Great Slave lake. Other geodetic and legal survey parties were also in the area during the past summer. The Dominion Water and Power Bureau also carried out reconnaissance and field investigations of the power possibilities in the vicinity of Yellowknife and established a number of gauging stations on certain important rivers and streams. Hon. members will be interested in knowing that to provide for the increase in population at Yellowknife a new townsite has been surveyed.

And that is adjacent to the island?
47696-212J

Adjacent to the island, on the road to the airport. It will be appreciated that the two votes mentioned do not cover all the dominion expenditures being made to open up this part of Canada. The Department of Public Works has appropriated a considerable sum to construct a portage road from the St. Charles rapids to Great. Bear lake. The construction of this road will be completed in the near future.
That is on the Great Bear river?

On the Great Bear river, yes. Other funds have been provided by the same department to improve the Mackenzie river waterway which at present is a principal medium of transportation. An. active programme of dredging was carried out last summer on the Clearwater and Athabaska rivers. The construction of a special dredge is now under way which will be used in deepening the channel in the Athabaska delta and will be ready for use next year. Other expenditures are being made for the purpose of improving the wharfage facilities at Fort-Smith, and investigations are being carried out for the purpose of bringing about improvements in similar facilities at the principal points along the river route.
Every effort is being made by the government to lower the transportation costs into the territories. This is perhaps the most important problem that has to be dealt with. The members will recall that jurisdiction has now been given to the board of transport commissioners in reference to the water transportation in the Mackenzie river area.
They will have to cut down the freight rates.

That is the idea. This will permit a proper investigation of the existing water rates. In order to provide other means of transportation, an agreement has now been reached with the Alberta government for tht construction of an all-weather road from Grim-shaw, Alberta, to Hay river settlement on Great Slave lake.

Are they not going to rivu on to Mill's lake? My information is that at Hay river falls one route goes to the mouth of the Hay river and the other goes to Mill's lake, forty miles west of Fort Providence.
Of course that may be a matter which will be followed up later.
I know where that Grim-shaw road is.

Surveys are being made at the present time, and they will be able to start in next year. Approximately 300 miles of this
Supply-Mines and Resources

road is in Alberta, and 80 miles in the Northwest Territories. Under the terms of the agreement the dominion and the province will share jointly the cost of construction of the provincial section, the dominion will contribute an amount not exceeding two-thirds of the cost, and the province will contribute not less than one-third. The section of the highway in the 'Northwest Territories will be built entirely at the cost of the dominion.
That is north of the 60th parallel.

Three hundred miles is in Alberta and eighty miles in the Northwest Territories. It is expected that the province will be calling for tenders for the provincial section in a few weeks and active construction work will commence early next year. It is anticipated that the road will be completed by the end of the year 1947.

Has there been any increase in the population of the Northwest Territories? Perhaps the minister can tell us what the possibilities are of employment in that area for men who are being demobilized from the forces. Is any information available for these young men about their chances in the territory? I feel sure that Canada is not doing what she could do to develop that country. One has only to observe what is going on the other side of the north pole to learn that Russia is building large cities in an area which, I believe, has about the same climate and much the same resources as the Northwest Territories. Is the government taking any steps to try to develop northern Canada in the same way that Russia has developed northern Siberia?
The hon. member asked with regard to the increase of population. There is an increase, and it is likely to be greater in the near future.

About what increase has
there been?

About 1,500 people more in the Yellowknife district. That may be increased considerably elsewhere. However, that is the increase reported at this time, and it is expected that there will be considerably more in the near future. So far as employment is concerned, the companies operating there are in touch with the department for the employment of men. The employment of returned soldiers is of course part of the rehabilitation plan and they will get the preference. There are many projects to be dealt with so far as the Northwest Territories are concerned. I *realize, as the hon. member has said, that Canada is looking to the territory as one of the great hinterlands which must take care of 
many of our problems in the future, more especially in connection with employment. All of these matters are being dealt with in the dominion-provincial conference. Our department realizes the seriousness and significance of development of the Northwest Territories from the point of view of all Canada. If I am strong enough to get a larger vote for next year I shall provide more funds in the next estimates for these particular purposes.
Have any steps been taken to find out the type of development which Russia has been carrying on in Siberia?

I do not wish to say anything which might be misconstrued elsewhere. Our department has been making inquiries with regard to the matters of which the hon. member speaks, with not very great success in getting information.

Before the item carries I want to compliment the minister on what he has said. It will give a great deal of hope to the people up in that country. A few days ago I received a copy of the Blade a Yellowknife newspaper. I am sure that when I send the editor of that newspaper the copy of Hansard containing what the minister has just said it will help to allay the fears of the people in that country. The population of the Northwest Territories is now about 10,000 in the whole area around Yellowknife, Fort Smith, and the territory north from Fort Smith and down to Norman Wells and Aklavik. The paper is called the Blade. It is published by a vigorous editor, and I hope he gives the minister praise for his programme. Here is what the Blade says on its first page, November 20, 1945:
Northwest Territories Association
As announced last Saturday, the Northwest Territories Association is in process of formation.
This is potentially a great and growing section of Canada but its present potentialities and all hopes for its future may be destroyed if the Ottawa administration is not aroused from its comatose condition.
We must show those swivel-chair northerners-by-proxy that we must have a say in our own affairs.
I am sure that when the editor, John Murray McMeekan reads the Hansard which I will send him by air mail, he will see that Ottawa is now alive to the situation.
I think, perhaps, to keep Hansard right, I should add something to what the minister stated about the Grimshaw road. I have been over it, from Grimshaw to Notakewin, so I know what I am talking about. The end of the present hard gravelled road is Notakewin. From Notakewin up to Hay river, or

Supply-Mines and Resources
rather to Alexandra Falls on Hay river, is a winter road, a tractor road made during the last two or three years, thanks mostly to the Alberta government. They will be pleased, I know, that this government is now going to cooperate with them in making that a hard surface road, as it should be. At Alexandra Falls the road will divide like a V; one goes off to the right to the mouth of the Hay river, from which point, in the winter time, tractor traips will go across the Great Slave lake to Yellowknife. That is the reason it is being built. The other part of the V will go to Mackenzie river, to Mill's lake on the Mackenzie river and across the Mackenzie river on down to the town of Norman Wells. I hope the minister will keep before him the Norman Wells area too, because that is part of the Northwest Territories. I am sure he is interested in the welfare of that part of the country and in making winter transportation possible where there is none now. His participation in any such effort will allay the feelings of the people there about separation, or whatever it may be called, because I could read further articles out of this paper referring to the time of the American revolution and suggestions about this being the time for them to organize and get busy.
The reason for that road from Grimshaw is the fact that the Great Slave lake freezes solid, so much so that after the Mackenzie river opens in the spring there is no steamer transportation through Great Slave lake for two and three weeks later, because, the boats cannot get through Great Slave lake into the Mackenzie river. It is felt that when the road is completed', tractor trains going north from Grimshaw will take large quantities of supplies to Mill's lake on the Mackenzie river, and in the spring the Mackenzie river boats will take freight down the river perhaps a month earlier than they otherwise could if they had to go through Great Slave lake. The same would apply in the fall of the year. When the boats are coming up the river they cannot go through Great Slave lake because of the ice, but they could unload at Mill's lake and ship by tractor train through to Grimshaw on the Peace River road.

I wish to ask the minister a question in regard to YeUowknife, but before doing so I think I ought to make this observation. After listening to the member for Davenport, and in view of the experience he has had and the knowledge which he has brought to the discussions in this house, I suggest that there are many people across this country who have been awarded a fellowship in the Royal Topographical Society for much less than the hon. gentleman has done in the interests of developing the natural resources of Canada. What I had in mind was this. Yellowknife is becoming one of the large centres in the north. The people there were disfranchised in the last general election. As I understand the situation, by reason of their location they are being denied the right to exercise their vote. I know that strong objection has been raised by the people, and I trust that between now and some time in the next feiw months when electoral changes are being made the minister will bring to the attention of the appropriate department the necessity of doing something to remove the unfairness that now exists.
Mr. GiLEN: The hon. gentleman is referring to electoral representation?
Yes.

A townsite has been formed in that district and they have a council, three of whom are elected by the people and three appointed by the commission of the Northwest Territories and council. The whole matter of representation will have to hi taken care of in the very near future rather than over a long period, because it is expected that there will be a large inflow of people as that area develops. NaturaUy the whole question will have to be considered in the. light of government policy.
What is the population?
About three thousand.

In Yellowknife settlement itself there are about 1,500, and in the remainder of the Mackenzie district, there are about 2 500 white people. But people are coming in and are likely bo come in in much greater numbers in the future. The original townsite of Yellowknife was built upon rock, there being no ready facility for sewage disposal, but there happens to be a piece of land, near the present site, which is covered with good earth, and we have been able to create a townsite which has been surveyed. The people will live there in a reasonable degree of comfort. Altogether we are fuUy aware of the situation. We are seized of the fact that considerable expense will be involved in the future development of that district. All encouragement must be given by the department for the development of that district, because if one believes all the fairy tales one hears, it is apparently an Eldorado.
Supply-Mines and Resources

The population of
Norman Wells, Fort Smith and intervening points should be included, because they are all in that northwest area.
If the minister were a betting man I would wager that the population in the next few years will be quadrupled.

I do not wish to retard the progress of these estimates, but I want to go back to the question of the national park at Riding Mountain, because it involves policy and is a matter of great importance. It involves the handling of the natural resources of the country. I think the minister should make a better statement than he has given us. He is familiar with the situation, since the park happens to be in his own riding and next to mine, so we both have a great interest in it. I would ask him why it was that the Northern Trust company could get a contract for two limber berths wherein they could cut lumber at a price of $1 per thousand, while settlers living around the park, if they could get a permit, which is difficult, had to pay a higher price. I do not know what the exact price is at the present time, but we have some indication from a return here which gives the names of two persons who received contracts. These were Mr. Dewitt and Mr. Proskin of Sandy lake, and the contracts were entered into in 1940. They paid $4.35 for the lumber they cut, while the Northern Trust company has cut over seven million feet of lumber at a price of $1 a thousand.
Before this item carries I would like to know when these timber berths were contracted for originally and for what period of time. The minister has told the committee that the contracts were made before the area became a park and therefore nothing can be done about it now. I do not want to criticize him. He is new in the department, and no doubt there are some things which he intends to straighten out when he can. But I would point out to him that this is certainly one of the things that should be straightened out very soon, and the reply that nothing can be done about it is not at all satisfactory. After all, the forest is contained in a national park and is the property of the people of Canada. There is therefore no reason why a contract made some years ago at the ridiculous price of $1 a thousand for lumber should continue in perpetuity. I do not know how long the contract has still to run, but I suggest that the minister should move immediately to make an adjustment. If the local settlers who need the lumber badly-and they need it worst of all-cannot get a permit in some cases to cut for their requirements, why

should some big corporation have the privilege of moving into a national park and taking out seven million feet of lumber in the last five years which they sold at a very handsome price for the building of airports near Dauphin.
Some of it was probably exported. They got it for SI a thousand. Because I think it is important and pertinent to the argument
I	should like to put on the record some of the figures. To make it perfectly clear I shall quote some of the figures which were given to me in the return dated September
II	of this year. I shall include only one of the timber berths, No. 571. This berth was contracted for by the Northern Trust company. The figures are as follows: In 1940-41 they took out 2,889,606 feet at a price of $2,852.26. The committee will note that that works out. at $1 a thousand feet. In 1941-42 they took out 1,185,510 feet at a price of $1,187.16. In 1942-43 they took out 421,781 feet at $415.79. I wonder how many people tried to buy lumber in those years and. what price they paid for it. In 1943-44 they took out 507,900 feet at $507.90. In 1944-45 they took 908,839 feet at $908.82. The other berth is 551-D, and it ran at the same price.
In August 1945 I had occasion to write to the Department of Mines and Resources in behalf of some farmers who came to see me. They were seeking a permit to cut timber in an area described as Buck lake. I have the reply of the minister here and I shall put on the record that part of it which is pertinent to this discussion. He replied as follows:
I have your letter of the 4th instant, to which was attached a petition from fanners in the vicinity of Gilbert Plains, asking that some 200 acres of mature timber southeast of Buck Lake be opened up for cutting.
This matter is being taken up with Superintendent Heaslip, and as soon .as a report has been received from him I will advise you further.
I would assume that the report was not favourable and this area was not opened up. There may have been some reason for that, but in view of the fact that this company has been taking out timber for many years-I know for five years-at $1 a thousand, timber which belongs to the people of this country, and the settlers who live alongside of the park have not been able to get any. I think that a great injustice has been done. I do not think that the reply of the minister that this contract was entered into before the area became a park is good enough. The farmers who applied to get a few thousand feet of lumber will not be satisfied with that

Supply-Mines and Resources
answer. We cannot shrug it off and pass the buck, even though it is in connection with Buck lake.
Does the Minister of Mines and Resources approve the contracts which were made with the Northern Trust company? It is important that we know whether this same policy will be followed in the future. Does the minister approve selling the resources of this country at SI a thousand feet to large corporations at a time when the farmers who are living next to the resources cannot get permits to cut timber at all?

A contract is a sacred thing,
is it not?

Another thing that should be brought to the attention of the committee is that the Northern Trust company do not cut the timber themselves. They have not set up a saw mill; they have sublet this contract to a saw mill which is doing the cutting, and there you see again the whole operation that has taken place repeatedly in connection with our natural resources, especially the forests. Some big concern comes along and takes out a contract on a large berth of timber at a ridiculous price compared with what people have to pay for lumber. A dollar a thousand is a ridiculous price. It is throwing our resources away.
Even then they do not go to the trouble to employ people directly to do the work, to to bring the timber out. They sublet it to saw mills. They let them do the work. They let the local people go in and get the timber out of the woods and bring it to the saw mill, and then those same people have to go to the lumber yard to buy it. A great injustice is done there.
Does the Minister of Mines and Resources intend to make an adjustment in this contract? If not, does he intend to give this committee a statement as to how long this contract with the Northern Trust company has been in force? What is the total amount that has been taken out of the national park at Riding Mountain? Will that contract be continued for any considerable length of time? I feel strongly about this; I feel sure that a great many members of this committee feel as I do. The resources of this country belong to the people, and where we cannot share them all equally we can at least give fair and equal treatment to all in making use of them. If there is any preference at all it should be given to the farmers and settlers who live next to the park and who wish to go in and take out the timber under their own power. It is a crying injustice to allow a big corporation to go in and
take out timber at $1 a thousand when local people are denied the cutting of a few thousand feet for their own use.

The hon. member must understand that these contracts were entered into prior to the taking over of the national resources by the province some time before 1930. I have not the exact date. The terms of those contracts are stated. As a dominion we are bound to maintain and uphold the terms of the contract, and there is nothing we can do about it.
Why not cancel it?

We do not intend to cancel a contract which has been entered into, and when the cutting of timber has continued under the terms of the contract. As soon as the cutting is completed on any part of the area, that land is taken over by the dominion and becomes part of the park, but it is not possible at this moment for us to cancel contracts which have been solemnly entered into and on which the company has been working for those years. The contract will expire as soon as the cutting by the berth holder is finished.
The price that they may charge and the price that they obtain for it are matters on which we cannot regulate the company. I have every sympathy with the horn, member, and I have had the same complaints made by residents around there with regard to timber in the park. The timber in the park is budgeted as to what can be cut. The price is as stated by the hon. member; but so far as the timber berth contracts are concerned we are in this position; we have either to live up to the terms of the contract, or repudiate it. I do not think the government wishes to do that.

I am very sorry to have to differ from the minister. I cannot be satisfied with that kind of answer. In the first place the questions I asked were not answered. I want to know how long this contract has been in force, when it was entered into, and how long it has still to run. That was not answered. I also wanted to know whether the minister approved this type of contract, and whether it will be his policy in the future to continue to enter into such contracts in other places. If I may say so, with all due respect, the reply that we have to live up to our contracts, though it sounds all right, is not good enough. If we were to go back and Live up to every contract that was made since the inception of this dominion we would find ourselves in a peculiar position.
Supply-Mines and Resources

I have not the exact date when this contract was entered into, but I think I told the hon. member that it was entered into prior to the taking over of the natural resources by Manitoba, before 1930, and thereafter they must live up to the terms of the contract. As soon as the cutting is done the contract expires. When they are finished their cutting in any portion, then that portion is included in the park, and only after all the cutting is finished will the contract be concluded.

There is a great weakness in that reply, which is in effect that the contract may run as long as there is any cutting to be done. Offhand I do not know the size of these timber berths, and I do not know whether the minister knows it, but just let us suppose that this trust company decided to divide these berths into sections and cut only so much each year. It would be quite possible for them, through the natural growth of the forest, to continue this contract for the next fifty or one hundred years at $1 a thousand. I do not know whether the minister approves of that, but I most definitely disapprove of it; I do not think that is the way our natural resources should be handled. If the government find that the contract which has been entered into was not a wise one and is not now an equitable one, in comparison with the treatment given others, then it should cancel the contract and enter into a new one, or else give the settlers the right to use the forests for their own benefit.
Is the minister's department doing any reforestation in these sections or these cuttings? The minister did not mention that.
No; that comes under another vote.

But is that being done? The minister can answer that. I just wondered if the department were doing any reforestation after this cutting is done. Is slashing permitted, or is only the mature timber being taken?
Of course all the cutting is done under the supervision of trained foresters. There is no reforestation in that particular portion, though some is being done in other sections of the park.

Did I understand from the minister's reply to the hon. member for Dauphin that the contract under which the Northern Trust company is taking timber out of this park lasts as long as there is timber to be cut?
Yes.
That is the agreement?
Yes. The contract provides that as soon as the cut has been finished that portion of the park will come back under the park administration.

Does that contract
cover all the park?
Oh, no.
Just the berths that have been referred to?
Yes.
And they hold these contracts in perpetuity until all the cutting they wish to do is finished, or until all the timber is cut?

I would not say in perpetuity, because the park officials are very careful to see that they live up to the terms of their contract, and also to see that the work is being done in accordance with the regulations.
Was this contract entered into between the trust company and the federal government, or trust company and the province of Manitoba?
I understand they are acting for some estate.
And they entered into a contract with whom?
The dominion government.
Then it was this federal government that entered into the contract?
Yes, prior to 1930. Then in 1930, when the natural resources were taken over by the province, of course it belonged to the park, subject to the timber berth licences.

The minister mentioned the terms of the contract and said the park officials were anxious to see that they were carried out. I am not going to ask the minister to tell us the terms of the contract. I realize that would not be fair, and possibly he would not have that information on hand, but perhaps he can tell us this much. Is the contract only for the cutting of timber, or can they take out anything they wish from those timber berths? In other words, may they cut firewood and pulpwood, or anything else they wish?
I am told that it covers merchantable timber, subject to the terms of the contract.

And what does that
involve-anything that can be sold as timber?

Surely, but in accordance with the terms of the contract and regulations.

Supply-Mines and Resources

If that is the case it is even worse than I thought, because it means that as long as there is anything of value to cut in these two berths the trust company has a complete monopoly for as long as they wish. That is the most iniquitous type of contract that could be conceived. I cannot imagine the minister, with his ability and his evident progressiveness, wishing to continue or even tolerating that sort of contract. It should be repudiated.
What consideration did the federal government get for the granting of a contract of this type to the Northern Trust company?

I have no doubt it was put up for tender at that time, though I have not the particulars with me, nor have I a copy of the agreement. But a bonus would be paid, I presume. I shall get that information and inform the hon. member.

I should like to ask a question in connection with the granting of a timber permit. What qualifications must be possessed by a person or a corporation in order to get a permit? It seems preposterous that a company without any saw-mill equipment, for instance, should receive a contract to cut timber. I think some qualifications should be set out by the department before such a contract is given to anyone who wishes to obtain a timber permit.

The only permits now issued are settlers' permits for the parks; we are not issuing any more of the others. In reply to the hon. member for Dauphin, we are not likely to enter into contracts to give privileges to any company to carry on lumbering in the park.
I want to ask a question following that asked by the hon. member for Dauphin. Is that SI a thousand typical of all the contracts being let in connection with the timber resources of this dominion?
This contract was made over twenty years ago, and these were the terms then agreed upon.

That does not quite
answer the question. Is it typical of the contracts now in force, whenever made? Are there any lower than that or any higher than that, and if so how much lower or how much higher?
I have no knowledge of any lower or higher. All I know is that we are not issuing such permits now in our national parks.
Should it not be the policy of the department to do reforestation work in all cuttings in the national parks?
I agree.
I know around Dauphin the land is very sandy. I do not know how it is in the park itself, but unless reforestation work is carried on there it will be waste land in no time.
That is part of the policy of the parks branch, to carry out reforestation where there is no regeneration.

Is there any provision in the contract requiring the company to do reforestation work in that section, or is it simply a case of the company taking all the profit and then turning the stumps and sandy land back to the state, putting the state to the expense of carrying on the reforestation, as has happened in connection with many of our natural resources? I am surprised that the minister should defend this type of contract. If this is the method by which the natural resources of the country have been disposed of, I am prepared to say it is a crying shame.
The hon. member suggests I am trying to support such a thing. The very contrary is the fact. I would be against it; it is not done, and I would never be a party to it.
I am glad to hear that.

. Mr. GLEN: The three votes for forestiy in this year's estimates, totalling $438,330,

Supply-Mines and Resources
cover the restricted activities of the forest service and are on a slightly higher level than the expenditures during the preceding war years. The estimates were prepared many months ago when the war was in (progress. These sums do not reflect all of the expenditures, as considerable war work was done in our forest laboratories and1 experimental stations and paid for from the war appropriation. I should also point out that there is included in the war appropriation for this year an item of $132,000 for the forest service in connection with expenditures relating to the post-war reconstruction programme.
Canada is a forest country. With a population of only twelve million people it stands in third place amongst the nations of the world in output of forest products. As an exporter of the products of forest industry Canada stands first, and her lumber, newsprint paper, and allied products are consumed in more than sixty different countries.
The forest resources of Canada are immense in size and diversified1 in character. If Canadians are to reap the full value of their heritage, our forest lands must be brought into a state of continuous production. Widespread destruction by forest fires, injurious insects and tree diseases must be controlled and the productivity of the forest soils fully realized1.
Administration and protection of the crown forests lying within provincial boundaries is, and will continue to be, a responsibilty of the provncial authorities. There is, however, a strong national interest in the welfare of this important resource. Forest industries have played a major role in sustaining Canada's available balance of commodity trade. Being on an export basis they have always been subject to the violent fluctuations of world markets. They must be placed1 in as strong a competitive position as possible. The permanence of forest industries depends on the continuing availability of raw materials. The nation cannot afford to see forests, as a source of raw materials, dissipated1. Neither can it afford to lose other forest benefits, including opportunities for recreation for our own people, the attraction of foreign tourists, the protection of watersheds, which vitally affects the hydro-electric industry and the protection they afford to agricultural lands.
It is believed that the dominion could properly assist the orderly development of the national forest resources in two directions: first, by expanding activities for which it would be fully responsible and, second, by assisting, through provision of funds, to raise provincial standards in respect of the
(Mr. Glen.]
conservation, protection and development of the provincial forest resources. Such assistance might be considered with respect to the raising of provincial standards, in protection of forests from damage by fire, insects and disease; to provide assistance in the construction of new forest roads, stream improvements and other works needed to facilitate improved forest management and the extraction of forest products; and assistance to develop recreational and other facilities for the enjoyment of the public and the well-being of our fish, fur and game resources.
The dominion forest service is already engaged in the broad fields of research, in silviculture, forest protection, utilization of forest products and forest economics. It has been proposed that these normal functions should be expanded so as more clearly to fulfil the actual requirements of the times. Discussions are in progress with respect to functions the dominion forest service might properly fulfil with respect to the protection of forested watersheds of interprovincial importance and where the protection of heavy dominion investments along other lines may be involved.
It is hoped that the estimates for the next fiscal year will make provision for expanded activities of the dominion forest service which will be necessary in the post-war years. It will be appreciated by the members of the house that pending decisions being reached at the dominion-provincial conference, it is impossible to make any statement now as to the details of increased dominion assistance towards the conservation and development of our forest resources.
In connection with what the hon. member said in regard to directing the activities of young men toward this field of service in Canada, we will, and I think everyone would desire that this should be done, direct their activities toward it; because here is an area which has been sparsely populated1 in the past and which I think offers a promising field for young men. I am hoping that the universities will take this into consideration.
Will the minister indicate whether a young man with only secondary school education would have any hope at all? That was definitely indicated to me by the department only three weeks ago.

The provinces are training young men for their own forest services. I do not think the question of academic qualifications would enter into it so much as the specialized education that a man might obtain in the school or college.

I must have been misinformed.

that falls under provincial jurisdiction. I know there have been continual efforts to cooperate. However, I will not press the minister further if he has not the answer immediately available.
May I ask what is the size of the federal staff in the forestry service?

This vote, No. 141, is for the advancement of forest conservation in Canada generally. It includes cooperative undertakings in an inventory of the forest resources, investigations of forest conditions, and determination of rates of growth. In the economic fields, analyses are made of statistics secured from the bureau of statistics, provincial authorities and other sources in order that the trends of development of forest industries and of domestic and foreign markets and prices may be closely followed.
Considerable assistance has been rendered in the war effort by the personnel and services of the dominion forest service, in addition to personnel seconded to war departments.
Forest fire statistics for Canada show that for 1944 the total number of fires, 5,820, was almost 300 more than the previous ten-year average. Although the quantity of merchantable timber destroyed closely approximated the average figure, the value of the timber, young growth and other property lost in forest fires was fifty-three per cent higher than the previous' ten-year average. The total damage and costs, $7,413,055, was over $2,620,000 greater, and fire-fighting costs, $1,328,338-the highest on record-were over one-half million dollars greater than the previous ten-year average. Human agencies continue to be the greatest cause of forest fires, with forty-six per cent compared with the ten-year average of fifty per cent; railways with fourteen per cent are much higher than the average five per cent, probably due to the wartime increase in traffic, defective equipment and shortage of personnel.
The shortage of forest products has been impressed upon the general public as never before, owing to the demands for war material. This urgent demand, and especially the shortage of fuel wood, have focused attention on farm wood lots. As a result, farmers are interested in securing information on how they should manage their wood lots to make them pay and keep them in continuous production. In cooperation with the Department of Agriculture surveys of wood lots on experimental farms and illustration stations were begun in the maritimes during 1944 and it is proposed to continue and extend these surveys in eastern Canada during 1945^16.

In general the importance of proper protection and management of woodlands has been continuously urged by the forest service. There is urgent need for a continuity of action in directing the policy and methods of forest conservation.
Much valuable data gathered at considerable expense by field survey parties has accumulated, but owing to lack of staff for compiling purposes, the results of these surveys are still unknown. Forest surveys are of value only if the resultant data gathered are compiled promptly and the findings made known. To compile data at present in arrears, and that to be collected in field work during the coming year, eight full-time compilers will be required.
The increase mainly comprises annual salary increases for permanent and temporary employees and some reclassifications of junior employees, already made, approximately $2,400; the return of one forestry engineer previously lent to Department of Munitions and Supply, $2,700; temporary appointments to vacant positions, $12,900, includes seven compilers, $7,560, replenishing of exhausted stationery supplies and necessary renewal of instruments and field survey equipment $3,400, cost of living bonus and unemployment insure ance, $2,600, and $1,200 for increased cost of travelling, transportation and sundries. The gross increase is approximately $25,200 which is reduced by a reduction of about $1,600 in wages and allowances due to changes in establishment.
The leader of the opposition asked as to the size of the staff. There are at present on the staff, as of September 3, eighty-five permanent and 49 temporary employees, or a total of 134.

Just one other question. The minister has told us of the huge losses of our forestry resources from fire and other causes, a matter that I am sure is of concern to him as it is to everybody else who is interested in the conservation of Canada's forest resources. It emphasizes the need for both provincial and federal authorities giving attention to this problem.
The minister has given us his estimates under three main headings: General scientific, economic, and administrative services, which is pretty general; forest experiment stations, which is more specific, and forest products laboratories. The losses in, our forest resources fall largely under two heads, fire and disease, but chiefly fire. Restoration comes largely through natural reforestation and artificial planting. Can the minister tell us how much money the department is spending on reforestation, how much on fire prevention and

how much on disease prevention? The estimates may not. be set up in that way, but these are the things which I think we should be concerned about.

The leader of the opposition may not have noticed a release from, the Department of Reconstruction regarding the newly created forest insects control board which the Minister of Reconstruction issued on November 25 last, warning of the destruction of Canadian forests by insect life, particularly the spruce bud-worm, which destruction, the release stated, has already reached the proportions of a national disaster. The release goes on to say:
The present epidemic, unless controlled, may result in the loss of 35 years' supply of raw material for paper products representing an export value of some eight billion dollars.
The new 'board is headed by E. Menard, formerly chief forest inspector for Quebec province. On it are J. J. de G-ryse, chief, division of forest insects, agriculture department, and D. A. Macdonald, acting dominion forester, mines ,and resources department. The other *members, whose 'appointment is announced today, are:
J. A. Brodie, division of forest protection, Ontario Department of Lands and Forests; Doctor Lionel Daviault, chief, Quebec Bureau of Entomology; Major-General Howard Kennedy of Montreal, vice-president, Ontario Paper Company; C. D. Orchard, British Columbia deputy minister of forests; and Doctor G. H. Prince, New Brunswick deputy minister of lands and mines.
"The presence on this board of government representatives from the provinces most seriously affected by the insect epidemic augurs well for successful cooperation between the federal and provincial governments," said Mr. Howe^ "This is the first instance in which the dominion has taken the lead in trying to organize an effective joint attack on a serious forestry problem. In view of the importance of our forest industries, *it must not be the last."
The minister stated that the first task of the forest insects control board will be to gather as quickly as possible all pertinent information in connection with the budworm plague, which has -already devastated some 22,000 square miles of forest and is present in a total of about 250,000 square miles, or roughly one-third of the accessible productive forest area of the_ nation. "The board will prepare a comprehensive programme and then will endeavour to have as much as possible of the actual work done by permanent government departments, both federal and provincial," he said. "The government will underwrite research work both here and abroad. As soon as possible, research experts will be sent to the timber countries _ of Europe to investigate the possibility of securing natural enemies of comparable European insect species which may prove effective in control measures in this country."
The leader of the opposition had another question?

It may be that the minister cannot answer me now, but the statement he has just made prompts me to ask

another question. At the opening of my remarks I added the two figures the minister gave to show how much this department is spending in forest services, but apparently not all the forestry activities of the government are confined to this department. Could the minister inform the committee some time within the next day or two what is the total of the funds which are being spent by the dominion government, in whatever department, with respect to forestry? I understand that some of it is in the Department of Agriculture. It is possible that certain lines of forestry should fall there. The minister has just said that there is another item in the Department of Reconstruction for research work in connection with forestry. A question occurred to me at the time this last item was mentioned was why should a forestry item be in reconstruction; why should it not be in the forestry branch of mines and resources? Then, I am sure, the minister could have his officials tell us later, if not now, how much the dominion spends on reforestation, on fire prevention, and on disease prevention, in whatever department.
I shall be glad to get that information and give it later.

I may be under the wrong heading, but if I am I would ask Mr. Chairman, the indulgence of yourself, of the minister and of the committee in the question which I intend to ask.
All of us here in the last month have received full-page advertisements from the Toronto newspapers with respect to coal resources. In fact a newspaper prepared an address which might have been delivered by the Minister of Reconstruction to both houses of parliament-I am not suggesting that he did it, but they prepared something which he might have done. I think that was the last advertisement I saw. What I want to ask the minister is whether his department have made investigations as to the truth of the allegations in these advertisements. They are in short these: that in Alberta, on the Sheep river, there are immense deposits of coal. We do not need to worry about the truth of that; I have seen them myself. The deposits are amazing. Some time ago they called this coal "anthracite". I notice that in their advertisements they have dropped the use of that word and are now calling it a very hard coal, and I think that that latter may be a more nearly accurate description than the one which
they formerly used. The main thing I have in my mind is this. Here in Ontario you are paying for anthracite in the neighbourhood of $16 to $17 a ton, and these people say that once they get a railroad built of some sixty miles they can lay the coal down in the Ontario area at $12.50 a ton. If that be so, it seems to me that to do this would mean a very great deal to the eastern provinces of Ontario and Quebec and also to the Dominion of Canada. I realize of course that at present a royal commission is sitting and examining the subject of coal, and perhaps it will take this into account. But all hon. members, I am sure, have received letters with advertisements from this newspaper, and I thought the minister might be able to give us some information. May I, to assist him, say that I myself have heard that from between Kentucky and West Virginia there is a very good quality of bituminous coal which can be laid down in places like Toronto and Hamilton at $9.50 per ton. If that be so there should not be a great deal of worry about the anthracite situation here.
Will the minister, now or at some convenient time while his estimates are being discussed, give the members generally the story of this coal situation?
As I say, I may be speaking at the wrong moment; and I am not asking him to reply extemporaneously; but would he give us some little discussion of Canada's coal position?- granted that that is in his department: I may be wrong.

No representations have been made to my department, nor have we been interested at the moment, in that coal question, because of the fact that a coal commission is now sitting. I did see the statement which was in the newspaper, a whole page of it, dealing with the question of coal. I am very glad to see that the Minister of Reconstruction, who knows all about this coal question, is in the chamber, and I think I will leave it to him to answer that question.

Then perhaps the Minister of Reconstruction can tell me. Perhaps he can also tell me the distinction between very hard coal and anthracite coal. I do not know what it is. I thought that anthracite was merely a very hard coal. Surely the minister and his department must have analyses of these various coals. What we buy coal for is to get heat from it and we do not want to pack water and ashes long distances, which is what we are doing now. Our old friend Mr. B.T.U. is very prominent in this connection. Perhaps the minister
Supply-Mines and Resources

could tell us if the department has analyses of these various coals, including the deposits I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply

I say that the coal mines
of the west have been developed by private industry, and in ordinary times there is a surplus of coal produced in western Canada to take care of the requirements of western Canada. It is felt that for the government to finance the development of a coal mine at this time would not be warranted by the existing situation, or the future prospects of the coal industry.

I have been told that this coal can be laid down here at $12.50, but I do not know whether any examination has been made to determine the correctness of that statement. I met a gentleman in Toronto and he wrote down the figures on a piece of paper for me, but coal is not mined simply by writing down figures on paper. There is a good deal more than that to it. I thought the Department of Mines was the proper place to look to, but I should like to know if someone somewhere cannot give us an amplified statement on the whole fuel problem in Canada. I am not going to join those who suggest that the government should build sixty miles of railway or give any other assistance unless there is a sure market and that market is not going to displace some other Canadian product. I would not for a moment advocate anything of the kind. But if it be a fact that the 
coal can be laid down here at $12.50, then it is a matter of considerable interest, particularly to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. There is a new field opening up in Kentucky, and if they can lay the coal down at $9.50, we are wasting our time talking about it. But in the minister's department there must be someone who knows all the facts. I am sure Mr. Frank Neate, if he is consulted, will have pretty much at his fingertips the answers to the questions I have been asking.
Mr. Chairman, I have risen before-
We are dealing with vote 141, which is forestry and not coal. I would not wish to have a discussion on coal now.
Mr. Chairman-
Will the hon. gentleman pardon me for just a second? May I ask when I may have the information I am looking for? I knew I was out of turn, but I do not know where to get my oar in.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The position is that over fifty per cent of Canada's coal is imported, and imported coal is used largely in Ontario and western Quebec. Previously coal moved from the maritime provinces westward as far as the city of Toronto and on the north line as far as Sudbury. Additional demands for coal in eastern Canada, and particularly the reduction in output, due largely to loss of man-power in the mines, have curtailed the area of markets for Nova Scotia coal so that last winter we were actually railing United States coal into Truro, Nova Scotia. That market will undoubtedly expand again, There is a subvention for the rail movement of coal, but not for coal moved by water, which ordinarily does not need a subvention. For coal moving by rail there is a rail subvention that amounts to $2.50 a ton for coal delivered in Toronto. On the movement of western coal there is also a subvention. It is my recollection, subject to correction, that a subvention of $6 a ton is required to move coal from Alberta to Toronto. Larger quantities might have been moved had a rail movement been physically possible, because domestic coal in Ontario has been exceedingly short. It has been necessary to use substitutes, providing a proportion of anthrar'te and a proportion of lower grade fuels for the ordinary household. The difficulty during the war years has been that the railways were so heavily burdened with freight that they could not handle extra traffic in coal. This winter there has been a larger movement than in previous years, which has been due to a slackening in

Supply-Mines and Resources
the movement of wheat, but unfortunately the movement of coal from Alberta east is in the same direction as the heavy movement of wheat. If it were the reverse, the movement could be handled more efficiently. The movement to Ontario has been limited owing to the fact that the railways could not handle the volume of coal which we should have liked to bring into the province, even with the higher subvention.
The position of coal is one of acute shortage on this continent and in fact all over the. world. Lack of coal on the continent is a serious threat to the well-being of the people, and its production is stepping up very slowly indeed. There is a demand for every pound of coal mined at this particular time. The long-range prospects are not such as would indicate the desirability of opening up large new sources of production in Alberta, considering the fact that it can be marketed only in Ontario on the $6 a ton subvention, which I need not remind my hon. friend is more than twice the cost of mining the coal. I suggest that the $12 rate that he saw advertised as the price for coal in Toronto would be after the government subvention had been applied to the movement.
Only $2. I do not act for these people. I do not even know them.

And we met at the Brown Derby. Does that mean anything? As a matter of fact I have read these advertisements.
Now that we are dealing with coal we are faced with another problem. The minister knows that during the war years more Alberta coal went west than ever. A good deal was used for bunkering and a good deal was used in manufacturing establishments out there. With United States coal used to haul engines on the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, the use of Alberta coal was being pushed clear back almost to the Alberta border in some instances, and beyond Winnipeg on both lines. We know perfectly well that we cannot hold the position on the Pacific coast because the demand is not there and is not going to be there. The chief worry is to get back on these railways coming east. We worked hard for twenty years to get where we did instead of having the coal come to Fort William by water, pushing us back again. The minister appreciates my having given him an opportunity to deliver that speech to both
houses of parliament

I am sure they will read it in the other place-but we should have a statement from him.
Mr. Chairman-
Will the hon. member pardon me for a moment? We are considering the estimates of the Department of Mines. Is there any branch of the minister's department which assumes responsibility for coal?
Only so far as testing is concerned, not so far as general policy goes.
I am a kind man and I like to give my friends every advantage-
And how!

-and Howe too. However, to follow along the line of discussion of the hon. member for Calgary West, the minister replied that those people who are interested in this particular coal mining area had made no representation to the government. Perhaps the Minister of Mines and Resources is trusting to his memory as applied to his own term of office. This subject is not a new one. I am quite certain that interested people have made representation over the years. I believe my hon. friend's question can be answered by the Canadian fuel board; I am sure they have all the data on this particular coal.
With respect to the campaign that is being carried on, I doubt whether the minister's reply was just 100 per cent accurate. I do not think the campaign that is being carried on is an attempt to have the government finance the mining of this coal. The problem is that there is no railroad running into this particular district. As the hon. member has already said, there is a distance of about sixty miles without a railroad. I fancy the people interested do not think they are the ones who are particularly responsible to put in a railroad. The campaign is put on to arouse public opinion in respect of this coal. It is an exceptionally good coal. It compares most favourably with anthracite. I do not know all the technical and chemistry terms which may be used in the analysis of the coal, but there is no doubt that it compares favourably with anthracite coal. If Canadian people knew that they could get in their own country coal which is just as good as any coal they can get outside this country, it would be an admirable thing if some steps were taken, perhaps by way of some assistance from the government, in the matter of building a railroad so that the coal could be made available to the rest of Canada.
Supply-Mines and Resources

The minister is right when he says that this item should be under forestry. There was a time when there was a considerable appropriation to be voted for subventions on coal.
It is in another item.
Not in this department?

Not in this department
at all.
I do not quite hear my hon. friend.
It is not in this department at all; it is in another department.
I do not think so.
Subventions? Of course it is.

I do not think so; I think it is missing from the book. However, I may stand corrected. We used to discuss subventions on coal under the Department of Mines and Resources. If it is shifted, all right, but it does not appear in these estimates.

Before this item passes I desire to say a few words. I can assure the minister that I will not delay this item, but when the proper time comes I intend to say a few more words on it.
There has been quite an advertising campaign put on with regard to this coal. I have a whole stack of them here. It was my intention to speak at length on them, but I do not think I shall do so at this session because the session is drawing to a close. Quite a pressure campaign is being put on in advertising this coal. What steps are the government taking to see that the quality referred to in the advertisement is correct? If the government does not come to the assistance of this organization when they take up this venture and go into a selling campaign to sell shares in this mine, it may very well be that the shares will not be worth very much because of the difficulties that have been indicated.
I think this matter only goes to prove what has been said on several occasions, namely, the necessity of establishing a national fuel policy. Certainly what the hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member for Calgary West have said, is true. It is high time that we began to devise a national fuel policy for this country so that we could use our own coal in Canada. If we have the coal here we should be using it. My understanding is that this coal could be loaded at a cheap price which would enable it to compete with Pennsylvania coal coming from the United States.

It is advertised as a high-quality anthracite, comparable with any anthracite coal we are getting in Canada.
We have endeavoured to capture a good deal of the Ontario market. Since the war we have lost a large part of that market. It is going to be quite a fight to regain it. If there is any possibility of our regaining the eastern markets by the development of this coal every assistance should be given to that end. Because of its peculiar chemical qualities, low ash content and high B.T.U.S it is said to be a good coal. If we can develop a market in eastern Canada for this coal we should go out and do so, and develop a national fuel policy for Canada.

When the item comes

Item agreed to.
Land, parks and forests branch-
US. Land registry-Land registry, seed grain collections, administration of ordnance, admiralty and public lands, $55,394.
I should like the minister to give a summary of the amounts outstanding in connection with seed grains, which I understand covers the period from 1914 to 1920.

The explanation of this vote
is that it has to do with the conduct of a central office of record for lands owned or otherwise controlled by the Dominion of Canada; the administration of ordnance and admiralty lands, dominion owned public lands, timber and grazing on soldier settlement lands and on military reserves; the adjustment of seed grain, fodder and relief indebtedness, and the issuing of letters patent. The over-all increase of $2,879 is due to an additional amount required for cost of living bonus, annual increases, replacement of depleted sta-tioneiy stocks, together with a small amount for surveys which have been postponed from year to year and are now urgently required.
I should like to know the amount outstanding in connection with seed grains, particularly in Saskatchewan.
As at March 31 last the amount outstanding in principal was $2,525,263.99, and in interest, $3,613,841.15, or a total of $6,139,105.14.

These debts go back to
1914-20, and I would say that eighty per cent of the people originally concerned have either died or left the country; yet these advances remain registered against the land. In many cases it has gone back to preemptions and rough lands, and I think this is detrimental to the progress of the country. I would take it that it costs more to keep the records than probably will ever be collected under this head, so that I strongly urge that these amounts be cancelled, because they are of long standing.

What have the collections been during the last two or three years, and what has been the cost to the government? I was going to ask those questions in order that we might have the picture. I believe these advances have been cancelled for some years. I should like to know for what years these debts have been cancelled; for what years they have not been cancelled, and the reason for cancelling in connection with certain years and not cancelling in connection with certain other years.

I could not answer that question now without a good deal of research. The net revenue in 1944-45 for seed grain relief was $111,577.85. As to the other particulars, I shall have to get a statement from the records and give it to the hon. member.

I believe the minister said that the collections amounted to some $111,000, while the amounts owing total in the neighbourhood of $6,000,000, of which, if I followed him accurately, more than fifty per cent was accumulated interest. As the hon. member for Maple Creek has just mentioned, the government has liens against a good deal of land occupied by people who had no connection with the conditions from which the liens arose. The small amounts that have been collected were, I believe, paid simply because the people now occupying the land are in a little better shape, due to the war and war prices, and want to get rid of those liens on their land in order to dispose of it. The statement by the minister would indicate that it is going to be difficult to recover the entire $6,000,000, and like the hon. member for Maple Creek and the hon, member for
Supply-Mines and Resources

Melfort I would urge .the minister to give serious consideration to cancelling at least the interest. I believe the whole thing should be cancelled, but perhaps, that is asking too much. I would, however, ask him to give serious consideration to the cancellation of the accumulated interest, because it is a great handicap for people who think they have paid all their debts to find, when they ask for clear title, that the dominion government has a lien registered against their land.
I shall be glad to consider tha' question.
May I ask what it cost the government during the fiscal year 1944-45 to collect that total of $111,000?
The services of two clerks only.

Is there anything in the estimates this year to provide for the extension of Louisburg national park?

There is nothing in these estimates in that connection. As the hon. gentleman knows, these estimates were prepared some time ago. When most of the departmental estimates are being considered here, my province of Saskatchewan usually is honoured more in the breach than in the observance in connection with any large expenditures. The matter of collections, however, comes up quite frequently. At this time I wish to pay a tribute to the Prime Minister of Canada for the interest he has taken in the Prince Albert national park, the only one in our province. We are less endowed with beauty spots than are the other provinces, but the Prince Albert national park, which is situated approximately in the geographical centre of our province, experienced reasonably good development during the period the Prime Minister was member for the constituency of Prince Albert. I am hoping, of course, that though he has moved from Saskatchewan to the constituency of Glengarry, his interest and that of the department in our national park will remain commensurate with the recreational needs of our people. In this park we

have quite a chain of lakes naturally well stocked with fish, which I believe are replenished to some extent by the department, though how extensive that work may be I do not know. I am sure it would delight even the hon. member for Calgary West to come and do a spot of fishing in Waskesiu lake, and we also have good golfing and beautiful motor drives. At page 319 of the public accounts for 1944 I notice that in 1942-43 expenditures in relation to the Prince Albert national park amounted to $93,636, while in 1943-44 they totalled $67,797. Since the public accounts for the fiscal year just ended have net yet been published, I should like the minister to tell me the expenditures and also the revenues in connection with that park for the year ending March 31, 1945, and also an estimate of revenues and expenditures for the current year. Would the minister indicate also what expansions are contemplated for this year under the headings of forest protection, fish propagation, tourist advertising, highways, clearings and buildings?

The estimate of the amounts to be spent in Prince Albert national park
are:

Public services	 25,300
Stores and equipment	 11,100
Recreation	 4,900
