Those are the current
estimates?
Yes.
What were the expenditures last year?

I am informed that more than that will be spent because of fire fighting that is taking place. I have not the particulars for 1944-45 that the hon. member asks for, but I can supply them to him later.
They will be tabled?
Yes.

I should like to say a few words with regard to national parks generally, but in particular with regard to the great belt of national parks generally known as the Rocky mountain national parks, which include Banff, Jasper, Yoho, Kootenay, Assiniboine, all that great string of parks that run along the central mountain backbone of the rockies. It may be surprising to some hon. members to know that these parks comprise an area nearly half as great as that of all Switzerland. I am one of those eastern Canadians who unfortunately

Supply-Mines and Resources
did not know their own country until a few years before the war. I had travelled widely in most other parts of the world, but I had not been to my own mountains until 1936.
I speak in humility; but having had some experience with mountains elsewhere in the world', I think I can say without fear of contradiction that we have the greatest potential mountain playground in the world. If we will develop them we have possibilities that will rival the great Swiss Alpine resorts. I do not speak with a lack of knowledge, because I have stayed at many of those great Swiss national resorts. Therefore I should like to see this vote multiplied many times, and this should be done by next session.
In the normal pre-war winter the great resorts of Switzerland were visited by more Americans than by the people of any other country. The Palace hotel at St. Moritz at one time had sixty per cent of its guest list made up of Americans. These people had the money to spend and they went there because they could get the service they wanted. The other winter sports resorts of Switzerland were filled with Americans, British and a great number of Canadian tourists. With the Atlantic closed to ordinary tourist traffic, in fact with all Europe being closed to transocean pleasure tourist traffic from this continent, we have an opportunity of getting that business for our national parks. It is significant that Switzerland's whole economy was dependent on the tourist and hotel business.
We have a magnificent opportunity if we only act now. It will be necessary for the government to carry on most of the activities, but they should start soon. If I may speak in particular of our mountain national parks, up to the present they have been developed for two classes of people, the very rich easterner and the overnight cabin tourist. It is all very well to build de luxe hotels such as Banff Springs, Chateau Lake Louise and Jasper Park Lodge, which must charge $20 to $25 per day, but that is not the way to open up our national parks. That is not the way to provide an opportunity to the people who own these national parks to see them.
It is not enough to build a series of motor roads through our national parks. In fact it would be a hideous thing to do. The whole beauty and charm, the amazing variety of our Canadian Rocky mountains are seen only when you get off the main highways and really get into them. With all due respect to our railroads, you do not see the mountains from the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific. You see a little more, but not very much more, from the Banff-Jasper highway. But
to really see the Rockies you have to get into them, and the only way to get into them is by horse or on your own two feet.
At the present time the facilities for getting into our national parks available to the ordinary and common garden variety of human being, whether he be Canadian, American or any one else, are extremely limited. If you go in in the summer you must go to the expense of providing yourself with a train of pack animals; you must provide yourself with a place to sleep, a tent or teepe, and with fodder; this is an expensive business. If you go in in the winter there are at the most only four chalets where you can go to enjoy the skiing.
I suggest that this government should do what the Swiss and Austrian governments did to develop the Bermese Oberland and Tyrol. This government should start in the near future; in fact they should have started already, to erect a number of shelter huts on or near the main passes, for instance north and south of the Bow river and in the vicinity of the Jasper-Banff highway and in time the Yoho district. In that way a great territory could be opened up. There is one hut in the Mount Assiniboine area, but it is difficult to get at, also the Alpine Club Hut in the Little Yoho. There is also one chalet Sunshine Lodge above Banff and Mount Temple and Skoki in the Slate mountains near lake Louise; four small chalets in the world's greatest accessible ski terrain. Mr. Chairman, the challenge is terrific. We must develop this priceless heritage. Huts should be placed close enough together, so that the average tourist or skier or mountaineer could get from one to the other without too much exertion or without undergoing tremendous expense in getting an expedition together.
What has been done on the continent of Europe is this. Huts are built within easy distance of each other. They are built in many instances with government help or with the help of some national mountaineering club or national ski club, who run the huts and take responsibility for them. I do not say that the government should go into the business of catering to tourists by providing food and shelter, but they should see to it that these huts are built so that a great number of tourists can go into the mountains.
What are the conditions at the present time? I have received word in the last week that every room available for tourists in the Banff national park is already booked not only for the summer but for the winter season too. You cannot even get the most modest accommodation for next year. It is all completely booked. I am not speaking of the
Supply-Mines and Resources

Banff Springs hotel, which I understand is to be opened next summer, but of places where the average man, not the millionaire, can go. All these are booked solid for the next year. That shows the tremendous demand for holiday accommodation by people on the American continent, arising very largely in eastern America, who go out to the Rockies and spend a great deal of time there. The demand is there; it is an extremely valuable demand; it is a demand from people who know the world and many of whom have seen the Rockies and have found there some of the best mountaineering and the best skiing the world has to offer.
I want to talk about skiing for just a moment. Skiing has become the great Canadian national sport. As a matter of fact it is a world-wide sport. I think most hon. members would find that there are vast numbers of the coming generation who now ski rather than skate. Many of them do. We used to think of skating and hockey as the great Canadian national sports, but now I think it has come to be skiing. Certainly that is so in the United States and on the continent of Europe.
We have within easy distance of lake Louise an area which for downhill running compares very favourably with the famous Parsenn country near Davos in Switzerland. When I say that it compares very favourably I mean that you have from several of the peaks surrounding lake Louise a vertical descent of from four to five thousand feet. That is essential for mountaineering skiing. The Laurentians are excellent in their way, but when you can get a run down through vertical descent of between four and five thousand feet that, Mr. Chairman, is really skiing. I assure you, sir, that once a human being has enjoyed the thrill of mountaineering skiing, nothing else will ever satisfy him to the same extent.
To develop this area several things are required. The first thing is adequate trails cut through the timber. That is not an easy thing to do. The trails, not narrow trails but twenty feet wide would have to be cut so that they remained in good condition. You cannot cut a trail straight down a mountain. You have to cut them so that the average skier can get down without breaking his neck. That is one thing that is required. The timberline runs at about 6,500 feet, and the main Bow river is at about 5,000 feet. So that there will have to be a number of ski trails cut through the lower slopes of these mountains.
The next thing to be done to develop a real skiing resort is to provide some type of ski tow. I say this with a degree of sorrow

because I thought that the average skier was an energetic person and I find that that is not so. There are energetic skiers and there are those who are not. The average human being is lazy, and if he can be lifted to the top of the mountain by a ski tow, not only does he get there with little effort and arrive without being tired, but he can get in a great deal more of downhill running and there is more time to improve his technique. In that way he gets a great deal more enjoyment out of a week or two weeks' holiday. The construction of a funicular or ski tow is essential and there are many places where it could be constructed within easy distance of the main railway line.
Once you establish that type of ski resort, you will have an opportunity to rival the great ski resorts of the world. You will have a gold mine that will make many of our gold mines, even the big ones, look awfully poor pickings. I am not speaking about something I do not know. I have seen what the Swiss did at St. Mauritz and at Davos. I have seen what the Austrians did at St. Anton am Arlberg and Kitzbuhel. I have seen how they made skiing almost pay the national debt of Austria, and how they established the famous ski school of Hannes Schneider. They attracted people from all over the world to ski on those mountains. If they can do that at St. Anton in the Arlberg, which is difficult to get to, we can do the same thing; we can attract skiers to lake Louise, but only if we provide the facilities. I suggest that we are missing one of the greatest opportunities, particularly at this time, because the continent of Europe is closed; the Americans want to go somewhere in winter and we have just the country for them.
One word more. Before we can adequately develop our mountain resorts we must have a well-trained corps of mountain guides. We are doing nothing now to train mountain guides. Hon. members who may not have skied or climbed mountains like I have may not appreciate the necessity of having a well-trained corps of mountain guides. A mountain guide is not just a man who hauls you up a mountain at the end of a rope. He is an extremely skilled technician and has to know a great number of things. On the continent of Europe a mountain guide takes three to five years to train. He knows his mountain technique; he knows his glazier technique; he knows his skiing, and he also knows his mountains. But I wish to make this very clear, that because you have a guide trained on the continent of Europe-a Swiss guide or an Austrian guide-it does not automatically

Supply-Mines and Resources
follow that he will know Canadian conditions. Our conditions are different in many ways from those of Europe. You have to train our young men. Certainly we have to borrow from the great wealth of experience of Europe, including Switzerland, Austria and northern Italy, but we have also to see to it that there are produced in Canada every year a number of guides who know not only the summer technique and the winter technique, but who also can do the things which are peculiar to our conditions, who can take a pack train into the mountains, who know about feeding and living in the mountains; and this can only be learned in the Rockies.
It is no good to go over and get a Swiss guide, admirably trained as a mountaineer though he may be. We must have a new technique, and I suggest to the minister that one of the first things we must do is to establish a school for the training of mountain guides. Why do I emphasize this so much? If you bring tourists from the plains and cities into the mountains they are going to get into trouble. A mountain is wonderful but it is also dangerous. You can fall down it; you can fall off it, and you can have parts of it fall on you. If we allow untrained and unacclimatized tourists to start off into the mountains we shall have a lot of casualties; not only that, but our tourists are not going to enjoy themselves. Living in the mountains is a science, and unless we have men who are able to take these tourists-I do not like the word "dudes", because they are not dudes who go into the mountains, but they are untrained, even though they are accustomed to European methods-they are going to get into trouble; we shall have men lost on mountains, Lost in glaciers, falling down, hurting themselves, and we shall make life a mise-ry for our park rangers who have to go out and look for them. I suggest that the government should give serious consideration at the earliest possible opportunity to the establishment of a school for Rocky mountain guides.
We have an opportunity now to develop our national parks both for winter and for summer, to build them into an asset which will rival the great Alpine resorts of the world. Europe is closed and may remain closed to the Americans for possibly two or three years. We have mot much time. We should start at once to see to it that our Rocky mountains are developed both for the people to whom they belong and for the people who will come to them and will mean so much to the economy of Canada.

Before hearing the remarks of the hon. member for York West, I was going to say something on the tourist trade in connection with the park attractions we have in Canada. I shall now content myself with asking the minister one question, about the beautiful national park on Prince Edward Island. Is his department considering building a highway so that tourists can reach that national park? I understood that when the park was laid out the idea of the department was to build a highway to provide easy access to that beautiful national park.

The aim of the department is to have all possible roads built which will provide access to the national parks. But at the moment I have again to give the same statement, that these matters are the subject of discussion between the dominion and the provinces as to the contributions which will be made for these roads. From a departmental point of view we are anxious that every facility and every necessary road shall be provided; it is an aim with which we are entirely in sympathy.

I most heartily endorse what has been said by the hon. member for York West, and I should like to elaborate briefly on one point. The greatest need of our national parks-at least the ones in Alberta, and I believe the same is true of other parts of Canada-is low-priced accommodation. The people for whom the parks were primarily designed, that is the people of Canada, are for the most part not able to use them as national playgrounds because of the high cost of accommodation.
I took up this matter to a slight extent with some of the officials of the department and was told that it is impossible at the present time to provide any further accommodation there because of the shortage of building materials of all sorts. I should like to urge on the government, however, that at the earliest moment-and I think it could be started quite readily next spring-low-priced accommodation, put up either by the government themselves or by private individuals, should be developed to the utmost. If ordinary building materials are not available a considerable start could be made with the logs which are obtainable right there. Unless this is done, most of the people who would like to visit our national parks and enjoy them will be unable to do so.
I wish to direct one question to the minister. Some two or three weeks ago in the veterans affairs committee we passed a resolution requesting the Department of Mines and Resources to change the regulations governing
Supply-Mines and Resources

the letting of leases in order that veterans [DOT]may have priority. As I understand the matter, at the present time, under the provisions of the law, any lands which become available for building sites or business sites are let by tender to the highest bidder. This places the returned man at a serious disadvantage as compared with men having more money; and the tenor of our resolution was a request that those regulations be changed, for the meantime at any rate, and lands which are available or are made available for either house building or business purposes be offered to veterans before being put up to tender. Will the minister tell us whether that recommendation from the veterans' committee has received favourable consideration.

I have heard of the communication to which the hon. gentleman refers, and we are dealing with it now. We are considering what shall be done. There are some investigations to be made with regard to it, and in the very near future some decision will be arrived at.
Have any submissions been made to the department regarding the extension of. the Cape Breton national park? If so, are they under consideration?
Yes. That matter has been referred to the department and is being taken up with the province now.

What is the intention of the government in connection with Wainwright buffalo national park? This was a national park until the early years of the war, and at that time the animals were all slaughtered. The park is at present populated by prisoners of war. Can the minister give any information as to what will be done in the near future as regards the use of the park?

The park is under the control of the army, and until they relinquish it to us we are not in a position to know what to do. After they have got out and it has been returned to our control, we shall decide what is to be done with it.
Will it be returned to the Department of Mines and Resources?
Yes; it is a national park.

Could the minister not be more definite and1 direct in his answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Calgary East? Banff is the place where I live and where some people occasionally vote, and both those who vote and those who do not vote are anxious to know where the veterans will stand in that community. The minister has been kind enough to see me on two occasions and his officials

have treated me generously in the matter of information, but we have a situation there where, broadly speaking, there is no land available. The only thing we have is the odd lot which for some reason is put up for sale. The present method is to sell it by tender. The people are so anxious to get places that prices are paid much beyond anything we have ever known, which means that the returned man has not a chance. There is a unanimous recommendation from the largest committee in this house and certainly the one that has sat longest and given the greatest attention to the problem submitted to it. I do not know why the minister cannot give us a little more encouragement than to say that certain investigations have to be made and that the matter will be given consideration. That is, may I say, scarcely treating this grand committee with the deference due to the distinguished members of it-and that remark has no reference to myself. I am not on the committee. I personally know Banff men who are trying to stay at home and do something and they cannot do it. The department might give us a little more encouragement in that regard.

I should like to give the hon. gentleman the encouragement he desires, but it is not just as easy as he says. I understand that there are only a few lots which have become vacant. There is hope that we may get a piece of land from the Canadian Pacific, who are not using it now. A resolution was passed by the committee on veterans affairs, but the question is, what shall be done in order that the veterans may be protected? The first thought in my mind, as it is in all our minds, is that the veterans shall have the preference where it is possible to give it. When it comes to a question of private leasing, if the land were taken and1 released at an increased price we would be subject to criticism of all kinds with respect to such increased prices. So that it is not just as easy as it seems. However, I can assure hon. members that the matter will be dealt with equitably, having in mind of course the preference that will be given veterans, because none of us would get away from that.

You could
cover that without trouble by a restrictive covenant of sale.

That is one feature which
has to be considered. We are not neglecting the position. The hon. member may rest assured that I shall treat it in the manner that he would wish me to.

Does all the land surrounding Banff belong to the Canadian Pacific?

Supply-Mines and Resources
No.

I understand that the
Banff townsite cannot be increased.

Item agreed to.
Lands, parks and forests branch-
11,7. Administration of Migratory Birds Convention Act, $50,750.

What I have to say on
this pertains also to the next two votes. I notice in the details on page 116 of the estimates that the staff that has to do with the Migratory Birds Convention Act is small. I know that the members of that staff are capable men. The ones I have met are thoroughly qualified, but their salaries are very small, the highest being $4,020 a year. I have been wondering if the next vote 148, for which there are no details, is for an extension of the work under vote 147. In this connection I wish to refer for a moment to vote 149. I have been wondering why something was not taken off vote 148 and added to vote 149, but perhaps the minister has in mind increasing the vote for the Jack Miner foundation. The whole committee knows that he was the one man in Canada who initiated this whole business. I was glad to know that the Prime Minister of this country, before the death of that distinguished gentleman, had conferred upon him, through His Majesty the King, the O.B.E. That was highly commendable and it was as it should be. I hope the department will give to the late Mr. Miner's three fine sons, Manley, Edward and Jasper, more assistance than was given to Mr. Miner in his lifetime. They are a family who have consecrated their lives and their farms to this great work and they do not get the credit they deserve. There has been opposition to them from one place and another, and I am not referring to the government. I suggest that they should be given the unstinted support of the people of this country.
Jack Miner was a wonderful man. His three sons are doing a great work. When I think of the small vote being given to them after what they have contributed I am amazed. They contribute 14,000 bushels of com a year for feeding these birds. I have seen as many as 30,000 there at one time. A grant like this, and the very small amount that they get from the Ontario government, does not begin to give them anything in return for the time they have contributed. I know for a fact that the eldest son, Mr. Manley Miner, has on several occasions refused $15,000 a year to go to the United States to set up what they have done in Canada. I know the minister is warmly disposed toward the Jack
Miner foundation. Personally I shall support him in every effort he makes to see that they get fair treatment.

I support what the hon. member has just said. I did not hear the minister say that he would increase the grant to $5,000. That was the amount of money that the Miner foundation anticipated they would get from the department. Does the minister intend to increase that grant?

We are dealing with item 147. I intended to say a few words on items 148 and 149, but perhaps we can take them all together. I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport with regard to the grant to the Jack Miner foundation. I have had more letters from all sides of the house in connection with that matter than with regard to any other single item in the department. Every hon. member is imbued with the idea that this vote should be increased to where it was some time ago. As the committee knows, it was reduced during the war years. The representations that have been made to me are in entire accord with my own thought. When this vote comes up next year I am hoping that I shall be able to impress the treasury board to put it back to where it formerly was, namely, $5,000. I realize, apart from any question in regard to the work that is being done, that it is a source of attraction, none greater in the Dominion of Canada. I shall certainly use all the force that I have at my command to see that the amount is increased to $5,000.
The enforcement of the Migratory Birds Convention Act comes under whom?
It is under the jurisdiction of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Since we are taking the three items together, what is the $40,000 for?
To provide for control and suppression of forest fires in the national parks, and for carrying on those activities.
When the minister is making his submission to the treasury board next year, will he consider restoring the grant to the Alpine club?

Any hon. member who has visited the Labelle building must have been alarmed at what terrific damage fire could do

to this country's vast treasure house of plans, specifications, maps and reports in connection with all our lands all over Canada. I urge the minister to request the Minister of Public Works, and through him, the government, to put up a fireproof building of steel and concrete to house the map treasures of this country so that they cannot be destroyed by fire. I should like to make a few brief remarks in connection with the Indian affairs branch generally. Some time

Special War Revenue
ago the minister indicated in the house that the Indian Act would be revised at the next session, or at least that he wished to have it revised then, probably by a committee of this house. For some considerable time the Indians of Canada have been pressing for a revision of the act by a royal commission, and personally I think that would be preferable to having it revised by a committee of the house. In any event, I presume one course or the other will be followed, and the Indian Act will be revised at the coming session.
In the past the Indians have suffered under a number of injustices. I should like to mention particularly education and medical attention, When treaties were entered into with the Indians they were promised that their children would be educated, but unfortunately the dominion government has not lived up to that promise, in that adequate educational facilities in the form of schools have not been provided to look after the Indian child population of school age. On the Stoney Indian reserve at Morley, Alberta, for example, there are something like 165 children of school age. At the residential school there, with children sleeping on cots in the corridors, there is accommodation for only one hundred. I imagine the minister will state that additional accommodation is available at the residential school in the Edmonton area. This, however, is some 250 miles away; and if children were sent there they would be completely away from their families for some ten months of the year and, in addition, would be among a different kind of Indians, speaking a different language and so forth. The Indians themselves believe that the time has come when on most of the reserves they would be much better off with day schools instead of residential schools, and for some considerable time they have been pressing for the establishment of day schools. I do not know why the department has not acceded to their request in this regard, because in most cases it would be considerably less expensive than maintaining residential schools.
Another difficulty as far as residential schools are concerned is that the grant is not sufficient, I believe amounting to something like $175 per child per year. I am sure all hon. members will realize that approximately $17 per month is not enough to feed, clothe and educate a child in a residential school. As a result, the religious institutions which operate these schools have to try to scratch up the remainder of the money required, which in many cases they are not able to do, and the children do not receive the education they should.
From the medical point of view, on several of these reserves there are no hospitals. I would refer particularly to the reserve at Hobbema, Alberta, where there is not now and never has been a hospital. If the Indians there become ill they have to wait a week until the doctor, who comes from Wetaskiwin, makes his appearance. If he has a considerable number of Indians to look after he deals with as many as he can, as they stand in the queue. When his time is exhausted he goes back and those he has not seen have to wait for another week. If it is a serious case the Indian has to be taken to the hospital at Wetaskiwin, but no conveyance is provided for that purpose. In this connection I would recommend to the minister that something in the nature of a jeep ambulance, such as was used overseas so successfully, be provided for each reserve on which there are not good roads and from which the evacuation of seriously ill Indians at the present time is a difficult problem. The provision of such a vehicle on most of the reserves in Alberta would make it possible to save many lives which otherwise might be lost. The government has large .numbers of these vehicles at the present time, and I should think it would be a comparatively simple matter to have some of them transferred from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Mines and Resources and apportioned for this purpose.
On many reserves where some hospital accommodation does exist, there is no medical officer, and that is particularly the case since the beginning of the war. I should like the minister to tell us what provision it is anticipated will be made in connection with medical officers now that the war is over and that medical men will be in much greater supply than has been the case in recent years.

The explanatory note reads:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was agreed that I should say something about the purpose of the bill on clause 1 in committee.
The purpose of the bill is to carry out the very important changes in the excess profits tax which were mentioned in the budget and in the budget resolutions. It is a little difficult to go into the matter in detail unless we take up the sections one by one. On the resolution I explained, and I think most hon. members understand, that by this budget beginning with the 1st day of January next the 100 per cent excess profits tax with 20 per cent refundable is reduced to 60 per cent. That is a short and simple way of stating it. But if it were to be stated accurately I would have to go into decimals and figures as I did on the resolution. That is what I would call the main change in the Excess Profits Tax Act.
There is a change in the taxation of sole proprietorships and partnerships. The 15 per cent excess profits tax is removed entirely; and what was 100 per cent tax, with 20 per cent refundable, becomes a 60 per cent tax in the case of proprietors and partnerships. Then a very important change is the raising of the minimum standard profits for small businesses. It was formerly provided that $5,000 was the minimum standard profit. That is, even if a small business had before the war profits of, say $2,000 or $3,000, we would consider for excess profits tax purposes that its standard profit was $5,000. That had the effect of cutting down the excess which was subject to taxation. Now, that $5,000 is raised. The formula is this, that on the profits of 1946 and the subsequent years the minimum standard profits of taxpayers be increased

from $5,000 to $15,000, and that where a taxpayer's standard profits are on January 1, 1946, in excess of $5,000 but less than $25,000, they be increased by one-half the difference between their present amount and $25,000. That is an important change which is provided for by this bill.
The only other change of substance is the renewal of the exemption from excess profits tax of the profits of certain mines. Heretofore that has been applied to base metal mines and strategic mineral mines: it is being extended in this bill to precious metal mines and to industrial mineral mines. All that is provided for in this bill. I will explain the bill section by section as best I can.

In connection with the drafting of these sections, ordinarily I can read any book or paragraph I pick up, but I find that the first sentence in section 3 consists of eleven lines, and if you go beyond the colon you add another six, making seventeen lines in all. How the government expects the ordinary Canadian citizen to read such drafting as its brought before this committee I fail to understand. Surely something can be done to make it easier; surely this can be broken up into shorter sentences with less length given to every statement of fact. I believe it is an intolerable burden to ask the Canadian public to try to understand language like that. It is not English at all; it is a conglomeration of words.
That is the first point. The second point I wish to make is that although on page 2 there is only one resolution, or one section of the act, despite what we tried to get across to the government the last, time these resolutions were being considered; despite what the senate committee on the working of the income tax law has said, in no less than three places I see the words "in the opinion of the minister". I believe they will holler more loudly than ever if they do not know what the law actually is. The other day my colleague the hon. member for Calgary West quoted1 an old maxim, that it is better that nine guilty men should go free than that one innocent man should suffer. May I suggest to the minister another legal maxim which I think has great bearing here; it is better that the law should be certain than just. That is an old common law maxim, the reasons for which he will find in any good textbooks on legal maxims, such as Broome or any other writer. Business men will refuse to enter into transactions if they do not know exactly how their profits will be dealt with. That happens almost every day in the life of a business man. Personally I find very often that there is no time to find out from Ottawa what will happen if you are successful in your transaction, whether or not your profits will be all taxed away, and, as a result, frequently do not enter into the transaction. Therefore, often employment is not created. So I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to the maxim that it is better that the law
should be certain than just. Frankly I do not know what these sections mean; I have had no connection with them in business practice, and I fail to understand exactly what is meant by that type of English.

I would ask the minister if steps have been taken or are proposed to put electric energy developed under private enterprise on the same basis as regards federal taxation as electric energy developed by public utilities operating under a provincial commission? I raised this question in a previous session and pointed out to the minister the inequity, which I think he recognized, that at present exists. In Nova Scotia we are taxed by the federal government about $1,000,000 on the use of electrical energy. In the city of Montreal users of electrical energy are exempted $6,000,000 or more a year because the utility has been taken over by the province. That also applies to other places in Canada. Let me give a few figures.
The federal tax on privately operated companies amounted in the case of the Canada Electric Company Limited in 1944 to $61,087.47. I do not believe that this included income tax or excess profits tax. In the city of Halifax the Nova Scotia Light & Power company paid $558,519.86 in 1944. In the minister's own constituency the Kentville electric commission, operated under provincial commission, did not pay one cent. There is no fairness or justice in that. Private enterprise is certainly being penalized, and I feel strongly that steps should be taken also to exempt private enterprise and put it on the same basis. It is not the companies but the users of the electricity that pay this inequitable tax. Why should users of electricity in the county of Cumberland or in the county of Halifax have to pay these very heavy federal taxes when users of electricity produced by a commission operating under the province are exempt? There is nothing fair or just in that.
I might also point out unfairness with respect to telephone services. In provinces where the telephone service is operated as a public utility by the province no federal tax is paid. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick where the telephone service is operated by private enterprise the tax applies. I have seen recent figures showing that the telephone service in Manitoba would have paid $3,939,656 more in 1944 if the telephone service had been carried on by private enterprise, and the telephone service in Alberta, $4,063,228, but they are relieved from that taxation because the telephone service is operated' as a public utility in those provinces and is exempt from taxation. But in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick they have to pay the tax. I point out again, as I have done in previous sessions, that

it is most unfair. There is cheaper capital cost when it has been supplied by the provinces on public credit.
In similar undertakings which have been built up by private enterprise, as a matter of course the capital cost is larger, because they are not able to secure capital funds to develop these generating plants as cheaply as they do where the security of the province is behind these industries. I ask the minister if it is proposed to take steps, and, if so, when, to equalize the taxes on users of electricity. In my constituency we have three private enterprise companies, and their patrons should not be subjected to these very heavy taxes.

Dominion Succession Duty

May I just say to the minister, in regard to the whole matter of the taxation of corporations, privately owned and publicly owned, in the same field of business, that I think it is time we had some clarification and perhaps rectification of a matter which is serious. It is not just in one part of the country but in all parts of the country. It is not because the publicly owned plant can operate so much more cheaply, but because there is no contribution toward all the public services which must be maintained by the general taxpayer, or else because the cooperative finds that it is not subject to taxation, in competition with privately owned tax paying enterprise, it has happened this year, and it has happened for a number of years, particularly when the rates of taxation became so high, that the private company-creamery, or dairy, or bread company- had no alternative than to sell out to the cooperative; or, in the case of utilities, it very often had to sell out to the municipality. I have no objection to public ownership, and I am all for public ownership where it is more economical and where the public can get better and: cheaper service than can be rendered by private enterprise. But when private enterprise has to start with a handicap such as is imposed by taxation, the other competitor in the race having no such handicap, the race is unequal, and the result is that the revenue act is driving a great many private enterprises into the hands of either public bodies or cooperatives. The minister must find that already there has been an appreciable reduction in the tax base, because he loses a taxpaying customer, and this means that those who are still able to run in the private enterprise race must bear a heavier and undue share of the whole tax burden.
I hope the minister in the next budget will give some consideration to this matter, because I can tell him again, private enterprises all through the country are being forced out of business, having to adopt the cooperative garment or else sell out to some political body which will operate free of taxation. I think it is to his interest and to that of the Minister of National Revenue, as the tax-gatherer, that there should be some certainty in regard to this, and that the people who are endeavouring to carry on business should know they are competing on a fair basis. Let us have, on the one hand, private enterprise and, on the other, public ownership, and let the better man win.

speechtext:
The committee will observe that the bill to amend the succession duty act does not contain the provision giving effect to the first resolution under the Dominion Succession Duty Act as proposed in the budget. The proposal, which has been dropped, was to provide that no duty shall be leviable on the value of any pension or portion thereof which is receivable as taxable income within the meaning of the Income War Tax Act. Since introducing this proposal I have given further consideration to the implications of the proposed exemption, and I am withdrawing the proposal with a view to giving the problem further study. I might indicate to the committee the questions which have caused me some concern.
Dominion Succession Duty

The proposal was that taxable pensions should be exempt from succession djuty. This gave rise to the question of the treatment of non-taxable pensions. Also, if taxable pension annuities were to be exempt, the further question of whether the ordinary annuity which did not arise from a pension scheme as such should not have similar treatment, such as for example, an annuity left by a will presented itself. Furthermore, the question of life interests and their status for succession duty purposes raises itself once the question of granting exemption in respect of taxable pensions is under consideration.
In view of the far-reaching implications of the proposal to exempt taxable pensions from succession duty, I decided to withdraw this item at the present time and to review it further. I trust the committee will regard this action as reasonable in the light of the points I have raised. The bill, therefore, simply gives effect to the second resolution, which provides relief against what are called quick successions. That is the entire bill.

The minister has stated the objections, and certainly they do not seem negligible; but it might be worth while to know what the considerations were, and presumably they were weighty, which prompted him to bring the resolution forward and have it passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. It was the recommendation of the Ives commission that we do just this, exempt from succession duty at the date of death the value of taxable pensions. It was clear from the recommendation that they meant pensions payable under employer-employee plans, pensions in the narrow sense; that they did not mean it to apply to an annuity left by will or a fortiori to life interest, real property, an apartment house left by a man to his wife for life. They did not mean to cover all those. They based this recommendation apparently upon the theory that the pension did not really come to the widow from the husband, that it was part of the husband's pay which he took in this way. He gets a pension during his lifetime, and she continues to draw a pension until she dies. It came from a fund built up by contributions by employer and employee, and therefore there was no real succession at all.
If that is the theory on which it is based, that theory applies, of course, to non-taxable pensions as well as to taxable pensions. Let us say that we adopted that theory and applied it to non-taxable pensions as well as to those that are taxable. Then the test of taxability flies out the window; and yet the test of taxability is the test which the ordinary
[Mr. Ilsley.J
person would apply in his own mind. That is, the ordinary person would say, "If you tax the income why tax the principal? Why put a succession duty on if you tax the income?" That is the test which most people would apply in their minds. But if that is the test it is so far-reaching that it appals me. What about life interests? The result is, I suggest with deference to the Ives commission, that their reasoning is faulty, and I do not think that the premises lead to the conclusion to which they came. I took their recommendation and thought about it a long time, discussing it with the officials, and I made up my mind that it was not very logical, but that, since they had recommended it, perhaps I would recommend it also to the house. However, when I began to think of all the implications I decided that I would not go on with it this session and I am not proposing to do so.
Does the minister distinguish between contributory and non-contributory pensions in this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The recommendation here applied apparently to contributory pensions, employees' pensions, pensions payable to employees who have worked for an employer and have built up a fund while doing so. They say that what the widow gets she does not get from her husband but from a fund to which both employer and husband contributed and that therefore it is not true succession and should not be taxed. But they limit that to taxable pensions and I brought it in on that basis.

I do not entirely agree with the minister. I understand that a differential is made between the pension that is a contributory one, namely, a pension in which the employer and the employee have contributed over a period of years and a straight pension that is given to an old employee on account of good service, or a retiring allowance to which he has not contributed at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not taking any action, so that the question does not arise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; that is the principle of the succession duty act.

Dominion Succession Duty
This is a very important matter. May I ask what steps the minister proposes to take to deal with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Give it consideration before the next budget; that is all.

As I understand it, I think there is some question as to whether or not that would be a succession. Suppose the husband dies and the pension continues to the widow and she has to pay income tax on that pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

In effect, she steps into the shoes of the husband. In addition to paying that income tax, she now has to pay succession diuty. I think there is good reason for doubting whether or not there is anything passing, whether there is a succession that should be taxed. Is that not the basis of the recommendation in the report? The widow steps into the shoes of the husband?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if I understand my hon. friend correctly, if I understand what he means by that phrase, "stepping into the shoes", that is the basis of that recommendation. The reasoning is found on page 43 of the Ives commission report, and it certainly would lead to the conclusion that we should not apply the test of taxability.

It just strikes me that where the estate passes within five years for a second time our rates are still pretty high. I know of one case where an old gentleman and his wife drew a holograph will; both were copies of the same thing. The husband died and within two years the wife also passed away, and while the succession duty on the second party passing is going to be 90 per cenf of what it otherwise would have been except for the small relief afforded by this bill, may I ask the minister what similar provision as to percentage obtained, let us say, in Great Britain, or in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In Great Britain the relief against quick succession is confined to property consisting of land or of business, such business not being carried on by a company. The rates are as follows:	The estate duty is
reduced by 50 per cent when a second death occurs within one year, and so on.
The same schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just the same as ours; we took the British schedule. There is no consideration for the degree of relationship. The hon. member for Kindersley suggested that
probably it would be better if we limited it to class A and class B beneficiaries; that is, to those who were related. We looked into it and decided against that, decided to leave the legislation as proposed in the resolution so that it might be left by a deceased to a stranger or by him to another stranger and still be eligible for relief. I will not go into the reasons for that, but I think they make no such distinction in Great Britain, and the rates are a lot higher, of course, in those cases. Sometimes a stranger is really as close to a person who dies as a relative. He may not have any relatives, and so on. While I thought the suggestion of the hon. member for Kindersley was a very good one, I did not think we should carry it out.
The rates may be higher in Great Britain, but they do not have the double taxation of dominion and provincial succession duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I meant the rates for strangers are higher than for succession to relatives. In the United States full credit is allowed against the taxes imposed on the second estate for the tax paid by the first estate on an amount equal to the value of the property when such property can be identified as having been received from the first estate or can be identified as having been substituted for property having been received from the first estate within five years. There is no consideration for the degree of relationship.

Does that mean the
amount of the tax deducted from the value of the estate on the second passing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is what it does mean. Saskatchewan and New Brunswick are the only two provinces which have provisions of this kind granting relief with respect of quick succession.

The only reason I raised this question is that the people who know how to handle their estates and get proper legal advice do not, as a rule, find themselves subject to two sets of succession duty taxes within five or ten years. A life interest is passed on to the widow by a man who may have done very well in a certain form of business, but yet has not the necessary legal experience or does not retain a good lawyer in the drafting of his will. Perhaps he leaves all of his estate to his widow, and the widow gives it to the children in a few more years. Because they are careless or have not used any care in the drawing of their will they will fall foul of double taxation at a high rate. I feel it is almost unfair to trap them like this. They should be given some
Dominion Succession Duty

consideration because, as I say, it is easy to circumvent unfair double taxation if you seek proper legal advice.
Do you think they should circumvent it?
Certainly.

I am seeking some advice since I have the minister here, an excellent lawyer, and his advisers. A simple person like myself, who knows nothing about succession duties, has only one will. It was made a long time ago, leaving everything to my wife, assuming that she would be fair to my children who are now grown up. Obviously I should not leave myself in that position. We happen to be of the same age. Either one of us is apt to conk out within one, two or three years of each other. When we get that eighty per cent in the third year, is it not an invitation to alter a situation of that kind which is based on love and affection, which most marriages are and should be? Are we not rather driven to changes which perhaps are not natural? I do not know whether I express myself very well, but I believe the minister understands what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have never given it much thought, and I should like to get a little advice myself on what to do in a case of that kind. That is, you leave a life interest so that there will be only one succession?
That is right. You could avoid it in that way, could you not?

Why not make the law
fair, so that it will not catch people who are just careless?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This makes it less harsh than it was, and, I think probably goes as far as it should go at the moment.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
